"I should not now cultivate the semblances of the various pāramitās.
This is called the mental attention of non-desire for cultivation.
Next, one forms this thought:
"I should now diligently practice the true perfections.
This is called the mental attention of the desire to practice.
Next, one should form this thought:
"I must now sever all mental engagements that constitute obstacles to the perfections.
This is called the mental engagement of non-conformity.
Next, one forms this thought:
"I now desire to attain the perfections of the stage of receiving the prediction, and I desire to attain the perfections of the stage of certainty.
This is called the mental attention of "desiring to attain."
The verse says:
He resolutely practices future deeds, Constantly observing that the practices of others are fulfilled;
His faith and understanding are foremost in himself, Because he knows his own essence to be unsurpassed.
The commentary states:

This verse contains three types of mental attention (*manasikāra*): first, mental attention consisting of resolve; second, mental attention consisting of observing others; and third, mental attention consisting of self-excellence.
Subsequently, the Bodhisattva forms this thought:
I perceive that in all future realms of existence, I shall definitely practice all the perfections through wisdom and skillful means.
This is called the mental attention of "definite performance.
Next, one forms this thought:
I should now contemplate that when the great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions fulfill the various pāramitās, may I also attain fulfillment, for we share the same purpose.
This is called the mental attention that contemplates others.
Next, one forms this thought:
"I now have confidence that the various pāramitās I practice are the foremost among all practices."
Why is this? Because I observe that this essence is unsurpassed.
This is called the mental attention of "I am superior."
The verse says:
By means of these various modes of mental attention, when cultivating the perfections,
the bodhisattva at all times brings their roots of goodness to fulfillment.
The commentary states:
It should be understood that this verse summarizes the preceding meaning.
Having already explained the seeking of the cultivation of roots of goodness, the next section explains the distinctions in the seeking of the Dharma.
The verse says:
Seeking the Dharma means its increase, The superior intention and its vastness,
Being with obstacles as well as being without obstacles, And the various supernormal powers.
"Without body and yet having a body, Obtaining a body and possessing a full body,
With much pride and with little pride, And because of being without pride.
The commentary states:
There are thirteen types of distinctions in the quest for the Dharma.
First is the quest for growth, which means that faith is increased through correct hearing.
Second is the quest with superior intention, which means receiving the stream of the Dharma from the presence of the Buddha.
Third is the vast seeking, which refers to Bodhisattvas who have attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and thus fully hear the teachings of all Buddhas from afar.
Fourth is the seeking with obstacles, which refers to those at the initial stage of increasing their faith.
Fifth is seeking without obstruction, because it is the seeking of superior intention.
Sixth is seeking through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because it is vast seeking.
Seventh is bodiless seeking, because the wisdoms of hearing and reflection lack a substantial body (*dharma-kāya*).

Eighth is the seeking of the body of existence (*bhava-kāya*), which refers to the body consisting of the seeds of the cultivation of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) through the development of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Ninth is the seeking of the attained body (*prāpta-kāya*), which refers to the stages from the first to the seventh bhūmis.
Tenth is seeking with a body full [of pride], which refers to the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages (*bhūmi*).
Eleventh is seeking with much pride, which refers to the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*).
Twelfth is seeking with little pride, which refers to the first seven stages.
Thirteenth is seeking without pride, which refers to the final three stages.
Having explained the distinctions in seeking the Dharma, the causes and conditions for seeking the Dharma will now be explained.
The verse says:
Whether as form or non-form, as supernormal powers or the True Dharma,
as the marks and signs of excellence or the healing of illness— these are the causes of mastery and inexhaustibility.
The commentary states:

There are four causes and conditions for seeking the Dharma: first, for the sake of form; second, for the sake of that which is non-form; third, for the sake of supernormal powers; and fourth, for the sake of the True Dharma.
"For the sake of form" refers to it being the cause for the primary and secondary marks of physical excellence.
It is for the sake of that which is non-material, because it is the cause for extinguishing the disease of afflictions.
It is for the sake of supernormal powers, because it is the cause of mastery.
It is for the sake of the True Dharma, because it is the cause of inexhaustibility.
As stated in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra*:
"A bodhisattva seeking the Dharma possesses four conceptions.
The first is the conception of it as a sublime jewel, because its meaning is difficult to obtain."
Second, it is like the thought of excellent medicine, because it has the sense of eliminating illness;
third, it is like the thought of wealth, because it has the sense of not being dissipated;
fourth, it is like the thought of nirvana, because it has the sense of the cessation of suffering.
Because the Dharma is the cause for the adornment of the marks and signs [of a Buddha], it should be regarded as like a wondrous jewel.
Because the Dharma is the cause for extinguishing the disease of afflictions, it should be regarded as like an excellent medicine.
Because the Dharma is the cause for mastery over supernormal powers (abhijñā), it is like the notion of wealth;
because the Dharma is the cause for the inexhaustibility of the True Dharma (saddharma), it is like the notion of nirvāṇa.
Having explained the causes and conditions for seeking the Dharma, the following verse explains seeking the transcendence of conceptual discrimination:
The non-existence and existence of entities, their increase and decrease, Their identity and difference, and their individual characteristics.
Regarding "the conceptualization of names according to meanings," there are ten types.

The commentary states: There are ten kinds of conceptualization: first, conceptualization of non-existence; second, conceptualization of existence; third, conceptualization of superimposition; fourth, conceptualization of denial; fifth, conceptualization of identity; sixth, conceptualization of difference; seventh, conceptualization of self-characteristics; eighth, conceptualization of distinct characteristics; ninth, conceptualization of arising meaning according to the name; and tenth, conceptualization of arising names according to the meaning.
In the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, ten types of remedies are taught in order to cause bodhisattvas to distance themselves from these ten kinds of conceptual discrimination.
To remedy the discrimination of non-existence, the Sūtra states: "There is a bodhisattva, a bodhisattva."
To counteract the discrimination of substantial existence, the Sūtra says, "One does not see a bodhisattva," and so forth.
To counteract the discrimination of superimposition, the Sūtra says, "Śāriputra, the intrinsic nature of form is empty."
To counteract the conceptualization of negation (*apavāda-vikalpa*), the Sūtra states: "Emptiness is not the cessation of form.
To counteract the conceptualization of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa-vikalpa*), the Sūtra states: "If form is empty, it is not form."
To counteract the discrimination of distinct characteristics, the Sūtra states: "Emptiness is not different from form; form is not different from emptiness; emptiness is itself form.
To counteract the discrimination of intrinsic characteristics, the Sūtra states: "This form is merely a name."
To counteract the discrimination of specific characteristics, the Sūtra states that form is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, and so forth.
To counteract the discrimination of objects as corresponding to their names, the Sūtra states that names are adventitious;
as with the name, one should not be attached to the object.
In order to counteract the discrimination that arises by naming things according to their referents, the Sūtra states that all names are invisible because they are invisible;
thus, one should not be attached to names as being like their referents.
Having explained the seeking of detachment from conceptual construction, next is explained the greatness of seeking the Dharma.
The verse says:
The Bodhisattva’s supreme valor Seeks the two truths to attain reality.
Conforming to all worlds, his merit is as full as the ocean.
Commentary:
There are three kinds of greatness in seeking the Dharma.

First is the greatness of skillful means (*upāya-mahattva*), because through supreme diligence one seeks the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) in their true nature, free from inversion.
Second is the greatness of benefiting others (*parārtha-mahattva*), because by acting as a refuge for the world, one establishes them in the ultimate truth.
Third is the greatness of self-benefit, because all merits are fulfilled like the ocean.
This concludes the "Chapter on the Quest" (*Paryeṣaṇādhikāra*).
*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.
Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra, Fascicle Six.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlabhadra of India during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen: On the Propagation of the Dharma. Commentary:
Having already explained the seeking of the Dharma, one should next expound the Dharma for others.
The verse says:
Difficult to obtain and yet not enduring, one who pities suffering always delights in giving;
how much more so when benefiting the world with the Dharma, for such growth is inexhaustible.
The commentary says:
This verse first refutes the stinginess regarding dharmas.
"Difficult to obtain and not firm" refers to body, life, and wealth.

"Compassionate toward suffering and always delighting in giving" means that out of compassion, Bodhisattvas are even able to relinquish these three kinds of non-firm things at all times to give to sentient beings who are afflicted by suffering.
How much more so for that which benefits the world through the Dharma and increases without end—how could one be stingy upon obtaining such a great Dharma that is not difficult to acquire?
Therefore, a bodhisattva should extensively benefit the world with this Dharma.
Why is this? Because the Dharma can increase and is inexhaustible.
Having refuted stinginess regarding the Dharma, the benefits are now explained.
The verse says:
Self-realization is ineffable; yet, to lead sentient beings, one speaks of the nature of phenomena.
The mouth of the Dharmakāya is quiescent extinction, yet its flow of compassion is like a python swallowing its prey.
The commentary states:

Regarding "the nature of phenomena taught to lead beings cannot be expressed by what is personally realized," the Blessed One did not speak of the dharma he himself realized, because it is inexpressible.
In order to guide and receive sentient beings, he further employs skillful means to expound the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Question:
What are these skillful means?
Answer:
The Dharma-body is quiescent, yet its mouth of compassion flows like a python inhaling.
The Buddhas take the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as their body and quiescence as their mouth; they are utterly vast and pure because they are free from the two hindrances.
Through great compassion, they emanate the net of the teachings to attract and guide sentient beings, just as a great python opens its mouth and emits saliva to draw in all manner of things.

The way all Buddhas, through the commonality of their compassionate body and speech, likewise attract and guide others is also like this; their great compassion is inexhaustible because it is ultimate.
The verse says:
Because they cultivate and attain the fruit, cultivation and teaching are not without purpose;
yet for those who merely hear or do not hear, cultivation and teaching would be without principle.
The commentary states:

Regarding the claim that cultivation and teaching are not without purpose because they result in the attainment of fruits—Buddhas employ skillful means to teach what they themselves have realized in order to guide the world; since practitioners attain these fruits through the sovereign power of their own cultivated effort, both that cultivation and the Buddha’s teaching are therefore not without purpose.

Regarding the statement that there is no principle for either hearing alone or practicing without hearing: if one could perceive the true meaning by merely hearing the Dharma, then practice would be of no benefit;
if one could enter into practice without hearing the Dharma, then teaching would be of no benefit.
Having already explained the benefits of teaching the Dharma, the distinctions in teaching the Dharma will now be explained.
The verse says:
"Teaching based on scripture and teaching based on realization, Which refers to oral expression and the power of supernormal faculties."
"Supernatural power refers to the primary and secondary marks, as well as other forms and space.
The commentary states:
There are two types of distinctions regarding the preaching of the Dharma by all Bodhisattvas.
The first is the teaching by scripture (*āgama*), which means speaking by the power of the mouth;
the second is the teaching by realization (*adhigama*), which means speaking by the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*).

There are many varieties of teaching by the power of supernormal faculties: some are spoken through the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), some through forest trees, some through musical instruments, and some from the midst of the sky.
Having explained the distinctions of the teaching of the Dharma, next the accomplishment of the teaching of the Dharma is explained.
The verse says:
Fearlessness and the severing of doubt, Causing faith and also revealing reality.
"In this way, the accomplishment of these bodhisattvas in preaching should be understood.
The commentary states:
The accomplishment of the bodhisattvas in preaching the Dharma is due to four kinds of meanings.
First is fearlessness, second is the severing of doubt, third is causing faith, and fourth is revealing the reality, as explained in the *Brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with four dharmas, they are able to open up the vast gift of Dharma. What are these four?
First, gathering and cultivating the sublime Dharma; second, the clarity and purity of one's own wisdom; third, performing the deeds of a virtuous man; and fourth, manifesting defilement and purity.
Among these, the first attains fearlessness because of extensive learning;
the second is able to sever doubts because of great wisdom;
and the third causes others to believe and accept [the teaching] because it does not rely on fame or profit.

Fourth, by means of penetrating the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one is able to manifest two kinds of reality: namely, the reality of defiled characteristics (*saṃkleśa-lakṣaṇa-tattva*) and the reality of purified characteristics (*vyavadāna-lakṣaṇa-tattva*).
The verse says:
Pleasant speech and freedom from intoxication, Absence of regression and absence of exhaustion,
Various modes and being appropriate, Causing understanding and not seeking profit.
"And through universal instruction, / Furthermore, the exposition of accomplishment.
The commentary states:
"Eloquent speech" means that when others respond with anger or abuse, one does not retaliate with harshness.
Regarding "being free from intoxication," there are two kinds of intoxication:
first, intoxication when praised by others;
second, intoxication when one achieves personal success, meaning the arising of attachment and joy due to the attainment of family, physical beauty, wealth, and so forth.
"Detached" means that these two types of intoxication have been extinguished within the mind.
"Without regression" means being free from indolence.
"Without anything remaining unexhausted" means teaching everything without the stinginess regarding the Dharma.
"Various" means that there is no redundant repetition.
"Correspondent" means that it does not contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).
"Facilitating understanding" means that the words and phrases are intelligible.
"Not seeking profit" means not causing others to have faith for the sake of material gain.
"Universal instruction" means it encompasses those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
Having explained the perfection of teaching the Dharma, the perfection of speech is now explained.
The verse says:
Not subtle and yet harmonious, skillful and also lucid,
appropriate to the occasion and free from seeking, measured and inexhaustible.
The commentary states:
"Not subtle" means it pervades the entire assembly.
"Harmonious" means it is pleasing to the mind.
"Skillful" means that the words and phrases are clearly elucidated.
"Lucid" means that they are made easy to understand.
"Responsive to capacity" means that they are taught according to what is appropriate.
"Free from seeking" means that one does not preach for the sake of fame or profit.
"Measured" means that there is no weariness in delighting to hear it.
"Inexhaustible" means that it cannot be fathomed.
Having explained the perfection of speech, next the perfection of syllables is explained.
The verse says:
"Upholding names and explaining meanings, Conforming to the vehicles and being gentle,"
Easy to understand and responsive to capacities, because it accords with and leads toward transcendence.
The commentary states:
Regarding the mention of the names, the various words and phrases are in accord with them because they do not contradict the evidence.
Regarding the explanation of meaning (*arthaviniścaya*): it refers to the words and phrases that explain [the teachings], for they do not contradict the principle.
Regarding the following of the vehicles (*yānānuvartana*): it refers to the words and phrases that follow the vehicles, for they do not contradict the three vehicles.
"Supple" means that it is free from difficult words and phrases because it does not contradict the sound [of the teaching].
"Easy to understand" means that by gathering together various words and phrases, the meaning is easily attained.
"Responding to capacities" means employing various words and phrases according to sentient beings, so as to suit their individual needs.
"Transcendence" means not remaining within those words and phrases, because one is directed toward nirvana.
"Conformity" refers to the correct practice of all words and phrases, because it conforms to the Noble Eightfold Path.
The verse says:
"The perfection of the Bodhisattva’s words should be understood according to the meaning previously explained."
The voice has sixty qualities; this explains the deeds of the Tathāgata.
The commentary states:
The Tathāgata possesses sixty kinds of inconceivable vocal tones, as described in the *Buddhaguhyasūtra*:
Śāntamati! The Tathāgata is endowed with sixty kinds of vocal qualities, namely: being moist, soft, agreeable, pleasing, and pure; thus it is explained at length.
In this context, "moistening sound" refers to the ability to sustain and gather the roots of goodness of sentient beings.
"Gentle sound" refers to the attainment of a pleasant touch upon hearing the Dharma in person.
"Agreeable sound" is so called because its meaning is virtuous.
"Pleasing sound" is so called because its syllables are virtuous.
"Pure sound" is so called because it is attained subsequent to the unsurpassed supramundane [wisdom].
The "stainless voice" is so called because it is dissociated from the habitual tendencies of all afflictions.
The "luminous voice" is so called because its words and phrases are easy to understand.
The "voice of virtuous power" is so called because it is replete with merit and destroys the evil, heterodox views of all non-Buddhists.
The "pleasing sound" is so called because it inspires faith, compliance, and renunciation.
The "uninterrupted sound" is so called because no outsider (tīrthika) is able to sever it.
The "subduing sound" is so called because it serves as the antidote to afflictions such as greed.
The "thornless" voice is so called because it delights in the skillful means of establishing the precepts.
The "non-grating" voice is so called because it enables those who have transgressed the precepts to achieve correct deliverance.
The "well-regulated" voice is so called because it provides instruction and guidance for the purpose of transformation.
Pleasant sounds are the antidote to a distracted mind;
sounds that provide physical support are able to induce samādhi;
and sounds that clarify the mind are able to induce vipaśyanā.
The "voice that gladdens the mind" is so called because it skillfully severs doubt.
The "voice that gives rise to joy and delight" is so called because it definitively uproots the heterodox.
The "voice free from feverish affliction" is so called because those who believe and accept it do not feel regret.
The voice that can sustain wisdom is the cause for accomplishing hearing, because it is the basis for wisdom.
The voice that can sustain understanding is the cause for accomplishing reflection, because it is the basis for wisdom.
The "unconcealed voice" is so called because it teaches the Dharma without stinginess.
The "lovely voice" is so called because it causes others to attain the fruits of self-benefit.
The "voice of yearning admiration" is so called because those who have already attained the fruits deeply aspire to and delight in it.
The "voice of instruction" is so called because it is the correct teaching of the inconceivable Dharma.
The "voice that causes understanding" is so called because it is the correct teaching of the conceivable Dharma.
The "corresponding voice" is so called because it does not contradict empirical verification.
It is a beneficial voice because it provides instruction and guidance as appropriate to each case;
it is free from redundancy because its speech is not in vain;
it is a lion’s voice because it strikes terror into the non-Buddhists.
The voice like that of an elephant is because it is majestic;
the voice like that of thunder is because it is deep and far-reaching;
the voice like that of a dragon is because it causes others to believe and accept it.
The voice of a *kiṃnara* is so called because its singing is beautiful;
the voice of a *kalaviṅka* is so called because its tone is clear and resonant;
the Brahma-voice is so called because it reaches far.
The voice of the Jīvajīvaka bird signifies that one first attains auspiciousness, for all undertakings are accomplished.
The voice of the celestial king signifies that none dare to disobey.
The voice of the celestial drum signifies the initial defeat of Māra.
The voice free from pride is so called because it does not become haughty when praising or censuring.
The voice that enters all sounds is so called because it enters all aspects of the *vyākaraṇa* (grammar and linguistics).
The voice free from incorrectness is so called because it is mindful and never forgets.
The "timely voice" arises because it initiates the work of teaching and transforming at all times.
The "shameless voice" does not depend upon gain or offerings.
The "fearless voice" is free from shame and embarrassment.
The voice of joy is so called because one never tires of hearing it.
The voice of equanimity is so called because it skillfully enters into all fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
The voice of a virtuous friend is so called because it accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings.
The "ever-flowing" sound is so called because it continues without interruption.
The "adorned" sound is so called because it manifests in various ways.
The "fulfilling" sound is so called because it preaches the Dharma through a single voice that produces immeasurable sounds.
The voice that delights the faculties of all beings is so called because immeasurable meanings are manifested within a single word.
The voice that does not disparage is so called because it accords with faith and compliance regarding the established meaning.
The voice that neither increases nor decreases is so called because it speaks in accordance with the appropriate measure of time.
The voice that is not hurried is so called because it does not speak too rapidly.
The voice that pervades all is so called because the assembly, whether near or far, equally relies upon it.
Regarding the term "accomplishment of all modes": it is because all worldly phenomena and their meanings are made understood through analogies.
Having already explained the accomplishment of syllables, next is explained the greatness of teaching the Dharma.
The verse says:
Exposition and designation, establishment and general summary,
detailed explanation and the severing of doubt— these cause understanding through both the concise and the extensive.
The commentary states:
"Expounding" refers to verbal expression;
"provisioning" refers to various phrases.
"Establishment" refers to being well-associated [with the truth].

Such analytical exposition, through both general summaries and specific explanations given according to their sequence, serves to sever doubts and render the meaning shallow, accessible, and easy to understand, so that those who hear and receive it may attain certainty regarding the Dharma taught.
The "abbreviated" refers to a single exposition, because those of sharp faculties attain understanding quickly.
The "extensive" refers to a repeated exposition, because those of dull faculties attain understanding slowly.
The verse says:
The speaker, that which is spoken, and the recipient—these three wheels are pure;
furthermore, being free from the eight kinds of faults, it should be known that the speaker is pure.
Commentary:
Regarding the purity of the three wheels—the speaker, the spoken, and the recipient—what are these three wheels?
First is the speaker, which refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Second is the spoken, which refers to the various categories such as names and so forth.
Third is the recipient, which refers to those who attain understanding through a brief exposition and those who attain understanding through an extensive exposition.
Furthermore, it should be known that the speaker’s purity consists in being free from eight kinds of faults; one should know that the speaker is pure and free from these eight defects.
Question:
What are the eight?
The verse says:
Laziness and lack of understanding, refusing requests and failing to explain the meaning,
as well as not severing doubt, severing doubt without firmness,
weariness and retreat, and stinginess— these are the eight kinds of faults.
The Buddhas possess no such essence; therefore, they achieve the unsurpassed teaching.
The commentary states:
the eight kinds of faults are, first, indolence; [and so forth].
2. not understanding the meaning;
3. rejecting requests; 4. not elucidating the meaning;
5. not severing doubts;
Sixth, because it eliminates doubt and indecision;
seventh, because the mind may become weary or retreat, as [the teaching] is not expounded at all times;
eighth, because there is stinginess, as [the teaching] is not fully revealed.
All Buddhas are thus entirely free from these eight faults; therefore, they achieve the unsurpassed teaching of the Dharma.
Having explained the greatness of the teaching of the Dharma, I shall next explain the accomplishment of its meaning.
The verse says:
This Dharma is excellent according to the occasion; it is the cause for generating faith, joy, and awakening.
Its meaning is correct and its expression skillful; it is able to open up the four Brahma-vihāras.
The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "this dharma, being excellent at all times, gives rise to the causes for faith, joy, and awakening," "excellent at all times" refers to being excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
Respectively, during the stages of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, it serves as the cause for faith, the cause for joy, and the cause for awakening.
Regarding "being the cause for awakening": it is because by observing the principles of these dharmas with a concentrated mind, one attains knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

Regarding "the correctness of meaning and the skillfulness of expression being able to open up the four Brahma-vihāras": "correctness of meaning" refers to the wholesome meaning and the sublime meaning, as they correspond to both conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Skillfulness of speech means being easy to receive and easy to understand, because the meaning is manifested through the clarity of the phrasing.
By means of this, one is able to reveal the fourfold holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Question:
What are these four?
The verse says:
Not associated with others, they fully sever the afflictions of the three realms.
"Intrinsic nature and stainlessness—these are the four kinds of conduct.
The commentary states:
The four sublime conducts (*brahmacarya*) are: first, solitude; second, fulfillment; third, purity; and fourth, whiteness.
"Not associated with others" means "solitary," because by means of this practice one does not associate with non-Buddhists.
"Fully severing the afflictions of the three realms" means "complete," because by means of this practice one fully severs the afflictions of the three realms.
"Essential nature" (svabhāva) means purity, because this practice is essentially pure by virtue of being untainted (anāsrava).
"Stainless" (vimala) means whiteness, because this practice attains stainless purity within the category of the body in which outflows have been exhausted (kṣīṇāsrava).
Having already explained the accomplishment of the meaning of the teaching, next the sections of the teaching are explained.
The verse says:
What are called the section on entry, the section on characteristics, and the section on remedies.
And the secret section—these are called the four sections.
The commentary states:

The Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma does not depart from these four sections: first, the section for causing entry; second, the section on characteristics; third, the section on remedies; and fourth, the secret section.
Question:
Upon what meaning do these four sections rely?
The verse says:
The Śrāvakas and their intrinsic nature, The severance of faults and the profundity of speech—
Based on these four meanings in sequence, There are four kinds of sections in the teaching.
Commentary:

Regarding the "sections for causing entry," one should know that these teach the various śrāvakas to enter into the meaning of the Dharma so that they may attain fearlessness, because it is taught that form and so forth exist.

Regarding the "sections on characteristics," one should know that these teach that all phenomena are without essence and without arising within the three natures—such as the imagined nature—and are pure by their very nature.
Regarding the section on remedies, it should be understood that they are based on the abandonment of various faults by means of counteracting eight types of hindrances.
As it is said in the Mahāyāna:
"By upholding two verses, one obtains such merit."
All these are taught for the purpose of counteracting [specific faults].
These countermeasures will be explained later.
Regarding the "secret sections," one should know that they rely on various profound expressions, as their meaning is only obtained through the transformation of the words.
As a verse in a Mahāyāna sūtra says:
"Understanding the non-solid as solid, Abiding well within the inversions, And being afflicted by the afflictions— One swiftly attains great bodhi."

Regarding the interpretation of "the firmness within the non-firm" in this section: "non-firm" refers to the undisturbed minds of all sentient beings; to form a firm interpretation regarding this state of non-distraction is the most supreme understanding, capable of attaining bodhi.
"Distraction" means that the mind is scattered and stubbornly attached, such that one cannot attain bodhi;
this is the meaning of the first phrase.
"Abiding well in perversion" refers to perversions, which are the attachments to permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

If a person can, amidst the midst of inversion, understand impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity, and dwell securely therein without regressing, they will be able to swiftly attain bodhi; otherwise, they shall not.
This is the meaning of the second phrase:
those who are tormented by afflictions attain enlightenment through long-term, diligent practice of difficult and painful austerities due to extreme exhaustion; otherwise, they cannot attain it.
This is the third point of meaning.
Having already explained the sections on the teaching of the Dharma, the intention behind the teaching of the Dharma will now be explained.
The verse says:
"Equality and distinct meaning, distinct time and distinct intention—
based on these four kinds of intentions, one should know that the Buddhas have spoken thus.
Commentary:

The Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma does not depart from four intentions: first, the intention of equality; second, the intention of distinct meaning; third, the intention of distinct time; and fourth, the intention of distinct desire.
As for the intention of equality, it is as the Buddha said:
"In the past, Vipaśyin Buddha was none other than my own self."
Because the *dharmakāya* is without differentiation, such explanations as these are called the "intention of equality.
Regarding the intention of distinct meanings, it is as the Buddha said:
"All phenomena lack intrinsic nature because they are unarisen."
Explanations such as these are called "intention regarding specific meanings" (*paryāyābhiprāya*).
Regarding "intention regarding specific times" (*kālabhiprāya*), it is as when the Buddha said:
"If anyone makes the vow to see Amitābha Buddha, they shall all attain rebirth [in his land]."
This is stated because [the result] arises at another time; such statements as these are called "intention regarding another time" (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*).

Regarding "intention regarding a specific desire" (*abhiprāya-abhiprāya*): a person possesses such roots of goodness that the Tathāgata may at times praise them or at other times disparage them, because they become satisfied with having obtained only a small amount of roots of goodness.
Such explanations as these are called the intention of specific desire.
Having explained the intention of teaching the Dharma, next the merit of upholding the Mahāyāna will be explained.
The verse says:
Disparaging the Buddha and disparaging the Dharma, Laziness and being easily satisfied,
The conduct of greed and the conduct of pride, Regretful conduct and instability—
these eight kinds of obstacles Are countered by the Mahāyāna teachings.
"When these various obstacles are severed, this person enters the True Dharma.
Commentary:
These two verses demonstrate the merit of severing obstacles within the Mahāyāna.
There are eight kinds of hindrances: first, the hindrance of disparaging the Buddha;

second, the hindrance of disparaging the Dharma; third, the hindrance of indolence; fourth, the hindrance of being easily satisfied with little; fifth, the hindrance of greedy conduct; sixth, the hindrance of arrogant conduct; seventh, the hindrance of regretful conduct; and eighth, the hindrance of instability.
In order to counteract the obstacle of disparaging the Buddha, Mahāyāna sūtras state:
"The Buddha Vipaśyin of the past was none other than my own self.
In order to counteract the obstacle of disparaging the Dharma, Mahāyāna sūtras state:
Only after practicing the Mahāyāna under Buddhas as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers does one attain understanding.
To counteract the obstacle of indolence, the Mahāyāna sūtras state:
"If there are sentient beings who vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, they shall all attain rebirth therein."
By reciting the name of the Buddha Vimalacandraprabha, one will certainly attain Buddhahood.
To counteract the obstacle of being easily satisfied with little,
Mahāyāna sūtras state that in some places the practice of *dāna* (generosity) and other virtues is praised, while in other places such practices are disparaged.
To counteract the obstacle of attachment-driven conduct,
Mahāyāna sūtras describe the supremely wondrous and blissful qualities of the buddha-fields.
To counteract the obstacle of pride-driven conduct, Mahāyāna sūtras state:
There are certain Buddha-fields of supreme accomplishment.
To counteract the obstacle of remorseful conduct, Mahāyāna sūtras state:
"There are sentient beings who, having committed harmful acts toward Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, are reborn in the happy realms."
To counteract the obstacle of instability,
Mahāyāna sūtras state that all Buddhas bestow predictions upon śrāvakas that they shall attain Buddhahood, and speak of the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
This is called upholding the Mahāyāna and attaining liberation from the eight obstacles.
The verse says:
Whether it be the words or the meaning, one who diligently receives and upholds these two verses possesses ten kinds of merit;
such a person is called one of supreme wisdom.
The seeds of goodness reach fulfillment; at the time of death, one’s joy is supreme.
One takes birth according to one’s wish, and the wisdom of recollecting births is perfected.
In every lifetime, one always encounters a Buddha, hears the Dharma, and attains faith and wisdom.
"Far removed from the two obstacles, one swiftly accomplishes the unsurpassed path.
Commentary:
These three verses demonstrate the merit obtained through upholding the Mahāyāna-saṃgraha.

These merits are of ten kinds: first, the accomplishment of a perfect basis for the seeds of all roots of goodness; second, the attainment of unsurpassed joy at the time of death; third, the attainment of rebirth according to one's vows in all places; fourth, the attainment of the wisdom of recollecting births (*jātismara*) by one's very nature in all places of birth; fifth, always encountering the Buddhas in the places where one is born; sixth, constantly hearing the Mahāyāna Dharma in the presence of the Buddhas; seventh, the accomplishment of the faculty of superior faith (*adhimukti-indriya*); eighth, the accomplishment of the faculty of superior wisdom (*prajñā-indriya*); ninth, the attainment of being far removed from the two obstacles of afflictions and knowledge (*kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa*); and tenth, the swift accomplishment of unsurpassed Bodhi.
If a person diligently receives and upholds even a single phrase—whether in letter or in meaning—from any of the Mahāyāna sūtras, they shall obtain these ten kinds of merit.

In this regard, it should be understood that one attains the first two kinds of merit in the present life, while one attains the remaining eight kinds of merit in future lives, which gradually increase and become more excellent.
Having already explained the merit of upholding the Dharma, the merit of teaching the Dharma is now explained.
The verse says:
With wisdom that is skillful and non-regressive, Great compassion and far-reaching renown.
Skillfully expounding all phenomena, Like the sun illuminating the world.
The commentary states:
If bodhisattvas are endowed with these five causes, they are said to be "skilled in preaching the Dharma."
First is teaching without error, due to the excellence of wisdom;
second is teaching at all times, due to non-retrogression;
third is teaching free from seeking, due to great compassion.
Fourth is teaching that inspires faith, because one's reputation is far-reaching.
Fifth is teaching according to the capacities of beings, because of skillful means.
By these five causes, one is able to preach the Dharma well, leading sentient beings to generate great reverence, just as the rising sun illuminates and brightens the world.
The Chapter on Propagating the Dharma is concluded. 14.
The Chapter on Following and Practicing. Commentary on the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, Chapter Fourteen, "Following and Practicing":
Having already explained the bodhisattva’s propagation of the Dharma, we shall now explain the bodhisattva’s practice in accordance with the Dharma.

Within this context of cultivation according to [the teachings], there is the knowledge of meaning, the knowledge of phenomena, following the phenomena, attaining together, and following in practice; these shall now be explained in their proper order.
The verse says:
Knowing there is no self in the two, And departing from both the false and the correct in the three—
A bodhisattva who understands in this way Is called one who knows the meaning.
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of meaning.
Regarding "knowing the two kinds of selflessness," this refers to knowing the selflessness of both persons and phenomena, because one knows that the grasper and the grasped lack intrinsic nature.

Regarding "the three [samādhis] that abandon the false and the correct": the "three" refers to the three types of samādhi, namely emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Through the samādhi of emptiness, one knows that there is no intrinsic essence, because one understands the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
One knows that there is no intrinsic nature through the samādhis of signlessness and wishlessness, because one understands the dependent and the perfected natures.
As for being free from the false and the correct: these three samādhis are not false because they induce supramundane wisdom, yet they are not correct because they belong to the mundane realm.

Regarding the statement, "A bodhisattva who understands in this way is called one who knows the meaning": if a bodhisattva knows the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena—and can understand the three types of samādhi as being free from both the false and the true, then such a person is said to know the meaning.
The verse says:
Having thus understood the meaning, one knows that the Dharma is like a raft;
one should not take pleasure in hearing the Dharma, for relinquishing the Dharma is called knowing the Dharma.
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies that the bodhisattva knows the Dharma.
Once the beginner bodhisattva has understood the meaning, he should next understand the Dharma.
This means that one should understand that the teachings of the sūtras and other scriptures are like the parable of the raft; one must not merely hear them and give rise to joy.
Why is this? Because these teachings are to be relinquished, just as a raft is.
This is called knowing the Dharma.
The verse says:
Ordinary beings possess two kinds of knowledge, which penetrate the two forms of selflessness.
In order to accomplish that wisdom, one practices in accordance with the Dharma as described.
Commentary:
This verse clarifies the bodhisattva’s practice in accordance with the Dharma.
Ordinary beings possess two kinds of wisdom: namely, the wisdom that knows the meaning (*artha-jñāna*) and the wisdom that knows the phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).

These constitute the penetration of the two kinds of selflessness; by means of these two wisdoms, they are also able to penetrate the two types of selflessness: that of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and that of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

Regarding the phrase "in order to accomplish that wisdom, one should practice in accordance with the Dharma as taught": in order to achieve those two kinds of wisdom, a bodhisattva should practice in conformity with the Dharma as it has been explained.
This is called "conforming to the Dharma.
The verse says:
When that wisdom is accomplished, it is supramundane and unsurpassed.
"Those who dwell in the first stage, / All that they obtain is obtained in common.
Commentary:
This verse clarifies the common attainment of Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the phrase "supramundane and unsurpassed when that wisdom is accomplished": this is because the essence of that wisdom is supreme.
As for the "first stage," it refers to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
This is because all the merits obtained by Bodhisattvas who dwell in the Stage of Joy are equally attained by one who has first entered that stage.
The verse says:
One should know that all afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing are completely eliminated;
subsequently, one cultivates the remaining stages in order to sever the cognitive obscurations.
One should know that within the various stages (*bhūmi*), there is no conceptual construction;
they arise in succession without interval. Thus it is said regarding their progression.
Commentary:
These two verses clarify the practice of the bodhisattva.

Among these, the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing are entirely eliminated upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*); therefore, the cultivation of the remaining stages is solely for the purpose of abandoning the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
However, each of the stages (bhūmi) possesses two kinds of wisdom:
first, non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna); second, the wisdom that establishes the stages.
When a bodhisattva is in right contemplation, they attain such dharmas at every moment without forming conceptual distinctions; this is called non-conceptual wisdom.

After the Bodhisattva has emerged from contemplation, he discriminates the dharmas obtained within that contemplation according to their respective categories; this is called the wisdom of establishing the stages (*bhūmi-pratiṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

These two types of wisdom cannot arise simultaneously, nor can they be interrupted by the arising of other dharmas; they proceed in constant, uninterrupted succession. This is called the Bodhisattva’s practice in accordance with [the stages].
When a bodhisattva is able to practice in this manner, there are four wheels of non-negligence:
first, the wheel of the superior land; second, the wheel of virtuous persons; third, the wheel of self-correction; and fourth, the wheel of prior merit.
Regarding these four wheels, they shall now be explained in sequence.
The verse says:
Easy to obtain and well-guarded, a good land and likewise good companions.
"In this supreme land of sublime tranquility, bodhisattvas are reborn.
Commentary:
This verse clarifies the wheel of the supreme land.
There are five causes and conditions for the excellence of the land:
first, it is easy to obtain, meaning that the four requisites for sustaining the body are not difficult to acquire;
second, it is well-protected, meaning that the king governs according to the Dharma, so that wicked people and thieves cannot dwell there.
Third is a favorable location, because the environment is harmonious and free from epidemics.
Fourth is favorable companions, meaning one has as associates those who share the same precepts and views.
Fifth is favorable tranquility, meaning there is no clamor during the day and a cessation of sound at night.
The verse says:
Extensive learning and vision of the truth, Skillful exposition and compassionate concern—
These four qualities of a non-regressing mahāsattva Are the supreme reliance for a bodhisattva.
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies the wheel of the virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*).
The virtuous person likewise possesses five causes and conditions:
First is extensive learning, because it accomplishes the Āgamas;
second is the vision of the truths, because one attains the fruits of holiness;
third is skillful exposition, because one is able to discern the dharmas.
Fourth is compassion, because of not craving gain.
Fifth is non-retrogression, because of being free from weariness.
The verse says:
Good conditions and a good assembly, Good cultivation and good teaching,
And good departure— these five kinds Are called the excellence of self-correction.
Commentary:
This verse clarifies the wheel of self-correction.
Self-correction also possesses five causes and conditions:
first, the condition of excellence, because the sublime Dharma serves as its condition.
Second is the accumulation of goodness, because it is fully endowed with merit and wisdom.
Third is skillful cultivation, because one cultivates during the times when the various practices of śamatha and vipaśyanā correspond.
Fourth is skillful exposition, because there is no seeking of profit.
Fifth is "skillful emergence," because one reverently cultivates all the sublime dharmas.
The verse says:
"Delightful and free from hardship, Free from illness and tranquil."
Observing these five kinds [of things], because of having planted roots of goodness in the past.
Commentary:
This verse clarifies the wheel of prior merit.
Prior merit also possesses five causal conditions:
first, being desirable; second, being free from adversity; third, being free from illness; fourth, meditative concentration (*samādhi*); and fifth, wisdom (*prajñā*).

The first matter has dwelling in a superior land as its cause; the second matter has encountering virtuous persons as its cause; and the latter three matters have one’s own correct accomplishment as their causes.
Having already explained the four kinds of wheels of heedfulness, next the emergence of afflictions from afflictions is explained.
The verse says:
Apart from the dharma-realm, there is no separate phenomenon of desire.
"Therefore, the Buddhas have taught: 'From greed one emerges; the remainder is likewise.
The commentary states:
As the Buddha previously taught, "I do not say that there is any dharma distinct from greed that can emerge from greed"; the same applies to hatred and delusion.
Because there is no separate essence apart from the dharma-dhātu, the dharmatā of desire and so forth receives the name "desire" and so on.
This teaching that the dharmatā of desire and so forth can transcend desire and so forth is the intended meaning of the sūtra.
The verse says:
Since there are no phenomena existing apart from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
it is therefore said that afflictions are themselves awakening (bodhi).
The commentary states:
As it is said in the sūtras, ignorance (*avidyā*) and awakening (*bodhi*) are one and the same.
This means that the term "awakening" is a designation for the *dharmatā* (the true nature) of ignorance; this is the intended meaning of the sūtra.
The verse says:
By giving rise to right reflection upon desire, one attains liberation from desire;
therefore it is said that desire emerges from desire. The same applies to the emergence from hatred and delusion.
The commentary states:

If a person applies correct contemplative observation toward desire and, having understood it thus, attains liberation from that very desire, it is therefore said that one transcends desire by means of desire.
The same applies to transcending hatred and delusion.
Having already explained how afflictions emerge from afflictions, next is explained the distancing from the minds of the two vehicles.
The verse says:
Bodhisattvas dwell in the hells, Enduring suffering for the sake of sentient beings without complaint.
To abandon existence and give rise to a small mind—this suffering is the most grievous.
The commentary states:
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, the Bodhisattva enters the great hells and does not shrink from great suffering.
If one extinguishes the merit of the three realms of existence by giving rise to the mind of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), for a bodhisattva this constitutes the most profound and heavy suffering.
Question:
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
Although one may constantly dwell in hell, it does not obstruct great enlightenment;
if one gives rise to a mind seeking self-benefit, that is an obstruction to great enlightenment.
The commentary states:
Although Bodhisattvas enter the great hells for the sake of sentient beings over a long period of time, they do not regard it as suffering. Why is this?
Because it does not constitute an obstacle to the vast and pure bodhi;
yet, if one gives rise to a mind that seeks nirvāṇa through other vehicles, this becomes a great suffering. Why is this?
Because it acts as an obstacle to dwelling joyfully in the Mahāyāna,
one should understand that this verse clarifies the meaning of the preceding verse.
Having already explained the prevention of the mind [seeking] the Two Vehicles, next is explained the prevention of the mind of fear.
The verse says:
Non-existence and perceptibility—this matter is like an illusion;
Intrinsic purity and stainlessness—this matter is like space.
The commentary states:
"That which is without substance yet is perceivable is like a magical illusion. All phenomena lack intrinsic nature; therefore, they are said to be "without substance.
Yet, because their appearances are seen to manifest, they are said to be "perceivable."
Ordinary worldlings give rise to mutual fear regarding these two points, but this should not be so.
Why? Because they are similar to illusions.

Just as illusions and the like have no real substance yet appear as visible phenomena, so too all dharmas are devoid of any obtainable essence; therefore, one should not feel fear regarding these two points.
Regarding the statement that "intrinsic purity and stainlessness are like space": the *dharmadhātu* is primordially pure, and is thus called "intrinsically pure" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*).
At a later time, it becomes pure through the removal of adventitious defilements, and is thus called "stainless" (*vimala*).
Ordinary worldlings give rise to mutual fear regarding these two points, but this should not be so.
Why? Because they are identical in their nature as emptiness.

For example, just as the nature of space is pure by its very essence, and is later described as being purified from dust, so too is the nature of the *dharmadhātu* pure and stainless. Therefore, one should not feel fear regarding these two points.
Furthermore, there is another simile of a painting that can dispel the two aforementioned fears.
The verse says:
"Just as a skilled painter Depicts the flat surface as having elevations and depressions,"
Such false conceptualization perceives subject and object within that which is non-existent.
The commentary states:
It is like a skilled painter who, upon a flat wall, can depict the appearance of relief; though there is no actual height or depth, one perceives height and depth.
Unreal conceptualization is likewise: within the state of non-duality in the equal dharma-realm, one constantly perceives the two marks of subject and object; therefore, one should not be afraid.
In this context, there is further a simile of water that can dispel the latter two fears.
The verse says:
"Just as clear water becomes turbid, / But returns to its original clarity once impurities are removed."
The purity of one's own mind is likewise so, for it is merely free from adventitious defilements.
The commentary states:
It is like clear water; when impurities enter, it becomes turbid.
At a later time, if it becomes clear, it is merely the removal of defilement.
This clarity does not come from without, for its original nature is clear.

It is the same with the mind’s purification through skillful means: the nature of the mind is originally pure, yet it is defiled by adventitious dust; at a later time, it becomes pure through the removal of that adventitious dust. This purity does not come from without, for its original nature is pure.
Therefore, one should not be afraid.
The verse says:
It has already been taught that the nature of the mind is pure, yet it is defiled by adventitious stains.
Apart from the *tathatā* of the mind, there is no separate purity of the nature of the mind.
The commentary states:

For example, just as the nature of water is inherently clear yet becomes turbid due to adventitious impurities, so too the nature of the mind is inherently pure yet becomes defiled by adventitious dust; this principle is already established.

For this reason, there is no separate, distinct mind apart from the *tathatā* (suchness) of the mind; rather, it is the *paratantra-lakṣaṇa* (dependent nature) that is described as being intrinsically pure (*prakṛti-viśuddha*).

Herein one should understand that when the *tathatā* of the mind is called "mind," it is precisely this mind that is said to be intrinsically pure; this mind is the *amala-vijñāna* (immaculate consciousness).
Having already refuted fear, he next refutes the fault of craving.
The verse says:
The Bodhisattva thinks of sentient beings, Loving them to the very marrow of his bones.
"Because they constantly desire to benefit [beings], just as if they were an only son.
The commentary states:
The affection that Bodhisattvas have for all sentient beings is termed "attachment."
The rest is as stated in the verse.
The verse says:
"By means of the intention to benefit sentient beings, arousing desire incurs no offense."
Hatred, however, is contrary to that, because it constantly desires to harm others.
The commentary states:
If it is claimed that a bodhisattva’s love for sentient beings constitutes the fault of greed, this argument is incorrect.
Why is this? Because this greed constantly acts as the cause for benefiting sentient beings.
The verse says:
Just as a pigeon feels extreme love for its own offspring, covering them everywhere,
so too does a person possessed of compassion feel such love for all living beings.
Commentary:
For example, just as a pigeon is full of craving and its affection for its offspring is especially intense,
so too is the Bodhisattva’s great compassion and his love for all sentient beings preeminent.
The verse says:
Loving-kindness is opposed to a mind of hatred; The cessation of suffering is opposed to a mind that seeks suffering;
Benefit is opposed to lack of benefit; Fearlessness is opposed to a mind of fear.
The commentary states:
Because a bodhisattva has attained a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, it is contrary to a mind of anger;
because he has attained a mind that brings relief from suffering, it is contrary to a mind that inflicts suffering.
Because they possess a mind seeking benefit, it is contrary to a mind that seeks no benefit;
because they possess a mind free from fear, it is contrary to a mind that creates fear.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva gives rise to such desire, it cannot be termed a transgression.
Having already refuted the fault of craving, the distinctions in practice are now explained.
The verse says:
One practices virtue within saṃsāra Like a patient taking bitter medicine.
Practice good conduct toward sentient beings, like a physician attending to the sick;
practice good conduct toward one's own mind, like training an untrained slave;
practice good conduct toward the objects of desire, like a merchant skillfully trading.
One who practices well in the three types of action is like a person who skillfully washes clothes;
one who practices well and does not harm others is like a father toward his beloved son;
one who practices well in cultivation is like one drilling for fire without ceasing.
Practicing skillfully in samādhi is like entrusting wealth to a trustworthy person;
practicing skillfully in prajñā is like a magician knowing his illusions.
This is called the skillful practice of all bodhisattvas within all spheres of experience.
The commentary states:
There are nine distinct types of practice for bodhisattvas.
First is the skillful engagement with saṃsāra; it is like a long-term illness where one takes bitter and astringent medicine solely to cure the disease, without giving rise to craving or attachment.
The Bodhisattva is likewise: he draws near to birth and death solely for the purpose of contemplation and self-exertion, not out of defiled attachment.

Second, regarding those who practice wholesome deeds: just as a skilled physician draws near to the sick, so too does the Bodhisattva; because of his great compassion, he does not abandon sentient beings afflicted by the suffering of afflictions.
Third is the skillful cultivation of one’s own mind: just as a wise master is well able to tame an untrained slave, so too is the bodhisattva, who is well able to subdue the untamed mind.

Fourth is skillful practice regarding the objects of desire; just as a merchant is skilled in trade, so too is the bodhisattva, increasing their wealth through the perfections such as giving (*dāna*).
Fifth, they practice the three karmas well; just as a skilled laundryman can remove stains and filth, so too does the bodhisattva cultivate and refine the three karmas, enabling them to become pure.

Sixth, practicing wholesome conduct so as not to afflict sentient beings: just as a compassionate father loves his young child and does not loathe them even when they are filthy, so too is the Bodhisattva; even when sentient beings cause him harm or loss, he never gives way to anger or resentment.

Seventh is the cultivation of virtuous conduct: just as one drilling for fire does not cease until heat is generated, so too the bodhisattva cultivates wholesome dharmas without ever allowing the mind to become distracted.

Eighth is the samādhi of skillful practice. For example, just as when one has wealth and employs a trustworthy steward, the assets increase day by day, so it is with the bodhisattva: by practicing various concentrations without distraction or attachment to their flavor, their merits increase.
Ninth is the skillful practice of Prajñā: just as a magician knows that his illusions are not real, so too does the Bodhisattva attain non-inversion regarding the phenomena he contemplates.
This is called the distinction in the bodhisattva’s practice.
Having explained the distinction in practice, next the purity of the three wheels is explained.
The verse says:
Constantly exerting great diligence, one brings the two to maturity and makes them pure;
with pure awakening free from discrimination, one gradually attains bodhi.
The commentary states:

Regarding "constantly exerting great diligence to mature both and bring them to purity": by means of the power of great diligence, the bodhisattva zealously practices the two benefits of self and others; thus, both sentient beings and oneself attain maturity, which is called purity.

Regarding "pure awakening without discrimination gradually attains bodhi": pure awakening refers to the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*). This wisdom does not discriminate among the three spheres—namely, the practitioner, the object of practice, and the act of practice—and is therefore pure.
Through this purification, one gradually attains unsurpassed enlightenment.
This concludes the Chapter on Cultivation according to Practice.
