Chapter Fifteen: Instruction. Commentary:
Having already explained the bodhisattva’s practice of cultivation, the instruction of the Tathāgata will now be explained.
The verse says:
Having completed one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, His long-standing faith increases further;
All manner of virtues gather through faith, Also becoming as full as the great ocean.
The commentary says:

Regarding "having completed one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, faith increases and becomes superior": when a bodhisattva has completed the practice of the stages for one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, at that time, their cultivation of faith reaches the highest grade.
Question:
Is it faith alone that increases?
Answer:
All manner of virtues gather according to faith and are likewise complete, like a full ocean.
That is to say, when faith increases, all virtues gather in accordance with that faith and attain fulfillment, just as the waters of the great ocean are serene and perfectly full.
The verse says:
Having accumulated merit, the Son of the Buddha is first purified;
possessing supreme wisdom and a gentle mind, he diligently cultivates all correct practices.
The commentary states:
"Having accumulated merit" refers to the accumulation as previously described.
"The Buddha-son is initially pure" means that he causes his protection to be pure.
Furthermore, they maintain upright views regarding the Mahāyāna because they do not misapprehend its meaning.
They are "extremely wise" because they have attained great learning (*bahuśruta*).
They possess "gentle minds" because they are free from all hindrances.
Because those who diligently practice the various correct conducts possess capability.
The verse says:
Thereafter, they receive from all Buddhas instruction through the stream of the Dharma.
Increasing the wisdom of tranquility, they advance toward the vast vehicle.
Commentary:

Regarding those who thereafter receive instruction through the flow of the Buddhas' Dharma, these bodhisattvas, from this point forward, receive teachings from the Tathāgatas through the *sūtras* and other dharmas, such as, for example, the teaching of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.

Regarding "augmenting the wisdom of tranquility and progressing toward the vast vehicle": if this bodhisattva receives instruction, they will augment their wisdom of śamatha and will be able to progress in the cultivation of the vast vehicle.
Having thus received the instruction, one next gives rise to six kinds of mental states.
The verse says:
Conceptualizing the name, as well as discerning the phrases, Contemplating the meaning, and knowing the meaning.
The Dharma is sought both collectively and by way of meaning; six types of mind arise in succession. The commentary states:

the six minds are, first, the fundamental mind; second, the accompanying mind; third, the investigative mind; fourth, the mind of realized understanding; fifth, the mind of collective synthesis; and sixth, the mind of aspiration.

"Conceptualizing names" refers to the fundamental mind (*mūlacitta*), which first observes that dharmas such as the sūtras have no dual meaning, because they are merely a collection of conceptual names.
"Comprehending phrases" refers to the subsequent mind (*anucāracitta*), which subsequently discerns the distinctions and sequences of the various phrases.
"Contemplating the meaning" refers to the mind of observation, because it subsequently engages in correct internal reflection upon that meaning.
"Knowing the meaning" refers to the mind of actual understanding, because it knows that contemplated meaning as it truly is.

The "comprehensive [mind] regarding phenomena" (*dharmasaṃgrāhaka*) refers to the mind that collects; it is so called because it further gathers the aforementioned phenomena and contemplates them collectively.
The "seeking [mind] regarding meaning" (*arthapravicaya*) refers to the mind of aspiration; it is so called because it seeks to attain understanding of the intended meaning therein.
Having thus given rise to these six mental states, one next gives rise to eleven kinds of attention (*manasikāra*).
The verse says:
There is seeking and there is contemplation; A single flavor, along with the path of cessation.
Contemplating the path and both together, Uprooting the sunken and suppressing the agitated,
Abiding correctly and without interval— In these, one also shows respect;
Placing the mind upon all objects, There are eleven modes of mental attention (*manasikāra*).

The commentary states: There are eleven types of mental attention (*manasikāra*): first, mental attention with both initial inquiry (*vitarka*) and sustained investigation (*vicāra*); second, mental attention without initial inquiry but with sustained investigation; third, mental attention with neither initial inquiry nor sustained investigation; fourth, mental attention of calm abiding (*śamatha*); fifth, mental attention of insight (*vipaśyanā*); sixth, mental attention associated with both; seventh, mental attention characterized by arousal; eighth, mental attention characterized by withdrawal; ninth, mental attention characterized by equanimity; tenth, mental attention of constant cultivation; and eleventh, mental attention of reverence.
"Accompanied by vitarka" refers to mental attention characterized by both vitarka and vicāra; this mental attention observes all phenomena through a continuous stream of mental verbalization.

"Accompanied by vicāra" refers to mental attention characterized by the absence of vitarka but the presence of vicāra; although this mental attention is free from vitarka, it likewise observes all phenomena through a continuous stream of mental verbalization.

"Single flavor" refers to the mental attention that is without vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought); this mental attention observes all phenomena in a continuous stream, free from the verbal expressions of the mind.
"The path of tranquility" refers to the mental attention of śamatha; this mental attention takes only the names of phenomena as its object.
The contemplation of the path refers to the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of insight (*vipaśyanā*); this mental attention takes only the meaning of phenomena as its object.
That which possesses both refers to the mental attention associated with both [calm abiding and insight]; this mental attention is able to take both name and meaning as its object simultaneously.
"Extricating the sunken" refers to the mental attention characterized by arousal; if this mental attention takes the name as its object and the mind becomes sunken, it is able to rouse and uplift it.

"Suppressing the agitated" refers to the mental attention characterized by withdrawal; if this mental attention takes the meaning as its object and the mind becomes distracted, it is able to hold it back and stabilize it.
"Abiding correctly" refers to the mental attention of equanimity (*upekṣā-manasikāra*); when the mind is balanced, this mental attention enables it to abide in a state of equanimity.
"Uninterrupted" refers to constant cultivation of mental attention; through this mental attention, one is able to cultivate based on correct abiding without interruption.
"Veneration" refers to the mental attention of reverence, which enables one to venerate the names and meanings during the stage of cultivation.
Having thus given rise to these eleven types of mental attention, one should further practice the nine ways of settling the mind.
The verse says:
Binding the object of focus, one should swiftly gather [the mind];
by internalizing and abiding in ease, one tames aversion and stills distraction; or likewise, one brings about arising and ceasing.
When the mind that performs actions flows of its own accord, one then attains non-action;
the Bodhisattva should further practice these nine stages of mental abiding.
Explanation:

The nine types of mental abiding are: first, the mind that abides in stability; second, the mind that abides in withdrawal; third, the mind that abides in liberation; fourth, the mind that abides in transformation; fifth, the mind that abides in suppression; sixth, the mind that abides in pacification; seventh, the mind that abides in cessation; eighth, the mind that abides in its own nature; and ninth, the mind that abides in maintenance.
These nine stages of abiding should be understood as the skillful means of instruction.
"Binding the object" refers to the mind being settled; it means settling the mind upon its object so that it does not stray.
"Swift withdrawal" refers to the mind being gathered and stabilized; it means that if one perceives the mind has become distracted, one swiftly gathers and sustains it.
"Internal withdrawal" refers to the mind of abiding; because one perceives that the mind is externally expansive, one further withdraws it inwardly.
"Delight in abiding" refers to the mind of transformation; because one perceives the merits of meditative concentration, one increasingly delights in abiding therein.
"Subduing aversion" refers to the mind abiding in subjugation; for if the mind does not find delight [in the object], it should be suppressed.
"Quieting distraction" refers to the mind abiding in stillness; for one sees the faults of distraction and causes them to cease.
"Or, arising and ceasing are likewise" refers to the mind abiding in cessation (*nirodha-sthiti-citta*), because as soon as greed, sorrow, and so forth arise, it causes them to cease.

"The mind that performs its own function flows spontaneously" refers to the mind abiding in its nature (*prakṛti-sthiti-citta*), because its activities are accomplished spontaneously through its own nature.
At that time, "attaining the state of non-action" refers to maintaining the abiding mind, because one attains dhāraṇī not through volitional effort.
Having thus cultivated and attained the abiding mind, one next causes this mind to attain supreme pliancy.
The verse says:
By relying on the lower [stages] and cultivating them to advance, one practices the fundamental concentration for advancement;
through pure dhyāna for the sake of supernormal powers, one shall accomplish a superior and supple mind.
The commentary states:

Regarding "cultivating lower tranquility and progressing toward higher training as the fundamental concentration," it should be understood that when a bodhisattva attains the state of abiding mind, they have already attained the lower grades of physical and mental tranquility (*kāyapraśrabdhi* and *cittapraśrabdhi*).
To further advance this reliance, one further cultivates the fundamental dhyāna-concentrations (*mauladhyāna*).
Question:
What is the merit of further cultivating the fundamental concentrations?
Answer:
Pure dhyāna is cultivated for the sake of the supernormal powers (abhijñā) so as to achieve a superior and supple mind.

Because bodhisattvas desire to give rise to the various supernormal powers and wish to accomplish the most excellent and pliant mind, they advance in the cultivation of the fundamental concentrations (mauladhyāna).
Question:
What is the purpose of giving rise to the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)?
Furthermore, how is the mind of supreme gentleness (*praśrabdhi*) accomplished?
The verse says:
Arising with supernormal powers, they travel through all realms;
They attend upon all World-Honored Ones, Attaining the most supreme and supple mind, Because they make offerings to all Buddhas.
The commentary states:

Regarding "arising of supernormal powers to travel through various realms and attend upon various World-Honored Ones," it means that bodhisattvas wish to go to immeasurable worlds, wish to pass through immeasurable kalpas, and wish to traverse the presence of immeasurable Buddhas; wishing to serve, make offerings to, and hear the true Dharma from them, they give rise to the various supernormal powers for these purposes.
Question:
For what purpose is this performed?
Answer:
Because one attains the most supreme and supple mind through making offerings to all Buddhas,
and by taking those offerings to the Buddhas as the cause, one further achieves the foremost, most excellent, and supple mind.
Having thus attained the superior mind, one then receives the praise of all Buddhas.
The verse says:
Before entering the pure mind, one attains five kinds of praise.
"Because the vessel-body has become pure, one is capable of advancing toward the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
The commentary explains:

Regarding the "five kinds of praise obtained prior to entering the stage of pure mind," this means that before reaching the Stage of Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*), this bodhisattva first obtains praise from the Tathāgata for five kinds of merit.
Question:
What benefit does this praise bring to a bodhisattva?
Answer:
Because the vessel-body has become pure, one is capable of advancing into the Unsurpassed Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*).
Once this bodhisattva has received the praise of the Tathāgata, they then achieve the state of a pure vessel-body and thus become capable of entering the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
Question:
What five virtues of that bodhisattva does the Tathāgata extol?
The verse says:
Moment by moment, all habitual tendencies are dissolved; Physical and mental dependencies, The perfect luminosity and its perceived marks— These constitute the pure and complete Dharmakāya.

Commentary: The verse states that through the continuous dissolution of all habitual tendencies (vāsanā), both physical and mental dependencies are eliminated. This results in the manifestation of the perfect luminosity (prabhāsvara) and its corresponding characteristics, thereby fulfilling and purifying the Dharmakāya.
The five merits are: first, the melting of habitual tendencies; second, physical ease; third, mental ease; fourth, perfect clarity; and fifth, the vision of signs.
"Melting away habitual tendencies" means that in each and every moment, one dissolves the entire accumulation of habitual tendencies.
"The body becomes supple" means that one cultivates pliancy until it pervades the entire body.
The same applies to the mind’s reliance.
"Perfectly luminous" means that one perfectly understands the emptiness of all aspects, because it is free from numerical distinctions.
"Seeing the marks" means seeing the mark of non-discrimination, as it serves as the cause for subsequent purification.
Regarding "fulfilling and purifying the dharma-body": this refers to fulfilling and purifying the dharma-body in all its aspects by constantly performing these five causes.
Question:
When is it fulfilled?
When is it purified?
Answer:
It is fulfilled at the stage of the ten bhūmis and purified at the stage of Buddhahood.

In this regard, one should know that there are five kinds of merit: the first three belong to the category of *śamatha*, and the latter two belong to the category of *vipaśyanā*. During this period, the bodhisattva attains full mastery over all worldly dharmas.
Having thus received such praise, he next gives rise to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
The verse says:
At that time, this bodhisattva / sequentially attains a concentrated mind.
"Because one perceives only mental verbalization, one does not perceive any objects.
The commentary states:

This bodhisattva, having first attained a concentrated mind free from mental verbalization, does not perceive any objects—whether their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—but perceives only mental verbalization.
This vision is precisely the Bodhisattva’s stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata); this stage is called "Clarity" (vidyā).
It is as explained in the Buddha’s *Kṣāranadī-sūtra*.
This clarity is termed the "receptivity to the vision of dharmas" (dharmanidhyānakṣānti).
The verse says:
In order to increase the light of the Dharma, one arouses firm and steadfast diligence;
once the light of the Dharma has increased, one attains penetration and abides in the realization that all is mind-only.
The commentary states:

Herein, in order to increase the light of the Dharma, the bodhisattva arouses firm diligence and abides in this light of the Dharma, thereby penetrating the realization that all is mind-only (*cittamātra*).
This penetration constitutes the "Summit Stage" (*mūrdhan*) of the bodhisattva.
The verse says:
All objects are entirely light, because one perceives that there is only mind;
having attained the severance of the delusions of grasping, this is abiding in patience.
The commentary states:

In this context, if a bodhisattva perceives that all objects are entirely the radiance of the mind, and sees no distinct perception existing apart from the radiance of the mind, at that time, the delusion of grasping is extinguished.
This view is precisely the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) for a bodhisattva.
The verse says:
Although the confusion of the grasped object has been severed, there still remains the grasper subject.
"Having severed this, he further swiftly realizes the uninterrupted samādhi.
The commentary explains:
herein, the bodhisattva, in order to sever the confusion of the grasper, further swiftly realizes the uninterrupted samādhi.
Question:
For what reason is this samādhi called "uninterrupted" (ānantarya)?
Answer:
Because one enters the "uninterrupted" state at the very moment the delusions of grasping are extinguished, it receives this name.
This entry into the uninterrupted state is precisely the Bodhisattva's stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Having explained the stages such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth in their proper sequence, the arising of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is now described.
The verse says:
Free from those two types of grasping, Supramundane and unsurpassed.
Non-conceptual and free from defilement, this wisdom is attained at this time.
Commentary:
"Far removed from those two attachments" means that the grasped object and the grasping subject do not coalesce.
It is "supramundane and unsurpassed" because it attains the Unsurpassed Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*).
It is "non-conceptual" because the conceptualization of those two types of grasping is absent.
It is "stainless" because the afflictions to be abandoned by the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) have been extinguished.
At that time, the bodhisattva is said to have become distant from dust and free from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
The verse says:
This is precisely the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), because one has attained the first stage (bhūmi).
After immeasurable kalpas, it becomes perfectly complete through reliance on purity.
The commentary states:

"This is the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) by which the first stage (bhūmi) is attained" means that this freedom from defilement is precisely the stage of the bodhisattva’s transformation of the basis.
Why is this? Because one has attained the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Question:
Is it based on ultimate purity?
Answer:
Only after passing through immeasurable kalpas does reliance on purity become fully perfected.

It is not that one attains ultimate purity at this very beginning; rather, it is only through subsequent passage of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas that this basis becomes completely pure and perfect.
The verse says:
At that time, penetrating the dharma-realm, the minds of others and one's own are equal.
This equality is fivefold, because the five are without distinction.
The commentary states:

Regarding "at that time, penetrating the equality of the dharmadhātu and the minds of others and oneself," it means that at the first stage (*bhūmi*), the bodhisattva attains penetration into the equal dharmadhātu.
By virtue of this penetration, they are able to perceive the bodies of others as their own body, and thus also attain equality of mind.
Question:
At this time, how many kinds of mental equanimity are attained?
Answer:
There are five kinds of equality, because these five are without distinction.
What are the five?
First is the equality of selflessness (*anātman*), which means not perceiving a self within one's own or another's continuum, as there is no distinction between them.
Second is the equality of suffering, which means that there is no distinction between all the sufferings existing within one's own continuum and those in the continua of others.
Third is the equality of action, which means that there is no distinction in the desire to eliminate suffering within one's own continuum and those in the continua of others.
Fourth is the equality of not seeking recompense, which means not seeking a return for what one has done for oneself or others, because there is no distinction between them.
Fifth is the equality of attaining together, meaning that whatever other bodhisattvas have attained, I too have attained in the same way, because there is no distinction.
The verse says:
All conditioned phenomena are false conceptualizations; pure wisdom realizes they are non-dual.
That which is to be abandoned through the vision [of reality] is liberation; thus is the path of seeing described.
The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are unreal conceptualization, and pure wisdom realizes their non-duality," herein the Bodhisattva perceives all conditioned phenomena within the three realms as merely unreal conceptualization, and through supremely pure wisdom, realizes that they are non-dual.
"Pure wisdom" is so called because it is supramundane.
"Non-dual" means that the two types of grasping are absent.
That non-dual essence is precisely the *dharmadhātu*.

Regarding the statement that "liberation is what is destroyed by vision" and thus refers to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), this means that liberation is the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*) through the path of vision.
The dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is itself liberation.
When one sees liberation and destroys the afflictions, it is said that the bodhisattva has first attained the path of vision.
The verse says:
Non-existence and existence-as-such, The intrinsic nature conjoined with the three emptinesses;
Understanding these three emptinesses— This is called the understanding of emptiness.
The commentary states:
Regarding the three kinds of emptiness: first, the emptiness of non-substantiality, which refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because its characteristics lack substantiality.
Second, the emptiness of semblance of substantiality, which refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because these characteristics lack substantiality just as the imagined nature does.
The three natures are empty; that is to say, the nature of reality (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is empty of its own essence because it is [itself] the essence of emptiness.
This verse reveals that the bodhisattva attains the gate of liberation of emptiness.
The verse says:
One should know that by taking the signless as an object, all conceptual constructions are completely exhausted;
herein, by taking the wishless as an object, unreal conceptual construction is exhausted.
Explanation:

The first half of this verse reveals the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*), and the second half reveals the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*); it should be understood that herein the bodhisattva fully attains these three gates of liberation.
The verse says:
The dharmas obtained at this time, all the factors of enlightenment—
one should know that those Bodhisattvas have attained them in the same manner as the Path of Seeing.
The commentary states:
"All factors conducive to enlightenment" refers to the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth; when that bodhisattva attains the path of seeing, he also attains these dharmas.
The verse says:
One awakens to the world as being merely conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), devoid of self and characterized solely by attachment to suffering;
when the meaningless "self" is extinguished, the Great Purpose relies upon the Great Self (*mahātman*).
Commentary: [As stated above.]

Regarding the realization that "the world consists only of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), which are selfless and only suffering": this means that the Bodhisattva realizes that all worlds are merely conditioned formations and truly lack a self; sentient beings' clinging is merely an attachment to suffering.
The extinction of the self that is devoid of meaning refers to the extinction of the defiled view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
"Great meaning" refers to benefiting all sentient beings.
"Great self" refers to taking all sentient beings as one's own self.

In this context, the bodhisattva eliminates the view of a self and relies upon the view of the "Great Self" (mahātman) to perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings; this is called "the great purpose based on the Great Self.
The verse says:
"No-self, yet the view of a self; No suffering, yet extreme suffering."
They benefit others without seeking recompense, because they seek their own benefit.
The commentary states:
herein, the bodhisattvas who are "without self" means they lack the view of a self that is devoid of its own welfare.
Furthermore, "the view of self" refers to the view of self regarding the great significance of other bodies.
"Absence of suffering" refers to the absence of various sufferings arising from one's own body.
"Extreme suffering" refers to the presence of various sufferings arising from other bodies.
"To benefit others without seeking recompense" means being free from expectation. Why is this?
Because one benefits oneself thereby.
When bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings, they are simultaneously benefiting themselves; therefore, they harbor no external expectations.
The verse says:
"One's own liberation is supreme, yet the bondage of others is firm and vast."
"The end of suffering is inexhaustible; thus one should apply oneself with diligence.
The commentary states:
"The mind that seeks its own liberation" refers to the cessation of those afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing within oneself.
"Supreme" means that this liberation is due to the Unsurpassed Vehicle (*anuttarayāna*).
"The bonds of others are firm and vast" means that they arise from the afflictions within the mental continuums of all sentient beings.
Regarding the fact that the end of suffering cannot be exhausted: it is because the realm of sentient beings is as boundless as space.

Regarding the instruction that one should thus apply oneself with diligence: since sentient beings suffer in this way, the bodhisattva should sever their suffering for the sake of those beings; having acted to bring about its end, they should act again and again, and must not rest.
The verse says:
If one cannot endure one's own suffering, how could one endure the sufferings of others?
One who reverses this attitude throughout this life and all future lives is called a Bodhisattva.
The commentary states:

Sentient beings are unable to endure the suffering of a single lifetime or the inconceivable suffering that extends to the very limits of saṃsāra; this bodhisattva, conversely, is able to endure all of these where others cannot, and it is for this reason that he is said to be the "contrary" of those [sentient beings], namely, the bodhisattva.
The verse says:
To practice equal love toward others, To benefit them without ever turning back—
This is neither rare nor not rare, For the benefit of others is one's own benefit.
The commentary states:

Regarding "practicing equal love toward others and not turning back from benefiting them," it means that a bodhisattva practices a mind of impartial love toward all sentient beings without distinction, whether seeking their happiness and benefit or actually performing acts to bring about their happiness and benefit.
When seeking to practice, the mind of benefiting others never regresses.
Regarding the statement "rare indeed, yet not rare, because it benefits both self and others": this quality of non-regression is the most rare and supreme among all things in the world.
Yet this rarity is not actually rare. Why is this?
Because when others obtain benefit, it is precisely the Bodhisattva himself who obtains benefit.
The verse says:
In the remaining stages, it is taught that one diligently cultivates the two knowledges through the path of meditation;
these are established as non-conceptual regarding pure phenomena and sentient beings.
The commentary states:
"The remaining stages" refers to the final nine stages.
Question:
What is cultivated in the remaining stages?
Answer:
Two types of knowledge are diligently practiced.
Regarding the two types of wisdom: first is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), and second is the wisdom that accords with what has been established (*yathā-vyavasthāpana-jñāna*).

Non-conceptual wisdom refers to supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*), while the wisdom that accords with what has been established refers to subsequently attained mundane wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-laukika-jñāna*).
Question:
What are the functional capacities of these two types of knowledge?
Answer:
Regarding pure phenomena and sentient beings:

herein, the function of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is to bring the Buddha-dharmas to maturity, while the function of the wisdom established [thereby] is to bring sentient beings to maturity.
The verse says:
During the stage of cultivation, for two asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one finally attains the empowerment;
entering that vajra-samādhi, one destroys all conceptual constructions entirely.
The commentary states:

Regarding "cultivating and establishing [the path] during the final stage of two asaṃkhyeyas to receive the empowerment," the "two asaṃkhyeyas" refers to the second and third great kalpas of the asaṃkhyeya; "final" refers to the ultimate stage of cultivation, wherein one receives the empowerment through skillful means during this stage of cultivation.
Question:
Having received the office, what further actions should be taken?
Answer:
Entering that vajra-samādhi, one destroys all conceptual discriminations completely.
Question:
For what reason is it called vajra-samādhi?
Answer:
Because it can destroy the analytical latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), this concentration is named "diamond-like" (*vajropama*).
The verse says:
The ultimate purity of the transformation of the basis, Accomplishing all aspects;
abiding here in these activities, Is solely for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Commentary:
"Ultimate purity of the transformation of the basis" means being forever free from all afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
"Accomplishing all aspects" means attaining the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), because it is unsurpassed.

Regarding "the activities performed while abiding here": this refers to manifesting the attainment of enlightenment and the manifestation of *nirvāṇa* while remaining in this state, until the very limit of the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) for all sentient beings.
Question:
For what purpose is this?
Answer:
"Only for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Such matters as these are exclusively for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings.
Next, it will clarify how one attains great benefit and profit by means of the great instructions.
The verse says:
The Honored Muni is difficult to behold; by beholding him constantly, one attains great benefit.
Through hearing the peerless Dharma, the mind is nourished by pure faith.
The commentary states:

This verse clarifies that, by virtue of the great instruction, a bodhisattva constantly attains the manifestation of seeing the Buddha, constantly hears the peerless True Dharma, and constantly gives rise to an extremely profound and pure faith that pervades the mind.
This clarifies that at the initial stage one attains great benefit and purpose.
The verse says:
If, within the instructions, One wishes to abide in the Dharma-gate,
"Just as one rescues others from perilous difficulties, so too does the Buddha exhort.
The commentary explains:

"If one wishes to abide in the Dharma-gates within the instructions, there are bodhisattvas who, at the time of receiving instruction, desire their minds to joyfully abide in the Dharma-gates of the Tathāgata."

"As when a person is pulled from a perilous difficulty, so too is the Buddha's exhortation. This is, for example, like a person who has fallen into a deep pit, and someone is able to seize him by his hair and toss him up onto a high bank.

The Buddha’s exhortation is likewise: if that bodhisattva delights in dwelling in the deep pit of quiescent extinction, the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, can forcibly place them upon the high bank of the fruit of Buddhahood.
This clarifies that at this subsequent stage, one attains great benefit and profit.
The verse says:
The world’s most pure eye, supreme awakening free from conceptualization,
is like the rising of the great sun, dispelling the darkness and illuminating the world.
The commentary states:

When Bodhisattvas attain Buddhahood, because they have forever transcended all mundane phenomena, their eyes achieve supreme purity; at that time, it is called the attainment of non-conceptual, supreme awakening.
For example, when the great orb of the sun rises, it can dispel the deep darkness and illuminate the world with brilliance.
This light ultimately brings about great benefit and profit.
Having explained this extensively, the preceding meaning is next summarized in a single verse.
The verse says:
The Son of the Buddha, having perfectly gathered and fulfilled [the provisions], achieves the most extensive meditative concentrations;
constantly receiving the instructions of the Honored One, he is able to fathom the ocean of merit.
The commentary states:
The meaning of this verse is as clearly manifest in the text.
This concludes the Chapter on Instruction.
Chapter 16: On the Companions of Karma. Commentary:
Having already explained the Great Instruction of the Tathāgata, it shall now be explained how a bodhisattva initiates karma with skillful means as its companion.
The verse says:
Just as the great earth, the source of all seeds, supports four kinds of things,
so too these three types of action establish all that is wholesome.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the bodhisattva’s skillful means for accumulating and initiating karma.
For example, regarding how the great earth sustains four kinds of things, what are these four things?
The first is the great ocean, the second is the mountains, the third is grasses and trees, and the fourth is sentient beings; these are called the four things.

Thus, regarding the establishment of all virtues through the three kinds of karma: the four things, such as the ocean, are metaphors for all wholesome dharmas. In this way, the three karmas of a bodhisattva can gather all virtues, namely the various pāramitās such as dāna and all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
The verse says:
Capable of performing deeds difficult to perform, manifesting forms throughout immeasurable kalpas,
with the very nature of body, speech, and mind, they pull others out [of suffering] without ever turning back.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the bodhisattva’s skillful means in the activity of rescuing others.
Regarding the phrase "capable of performing difficult deeds and manifesting forms for immeasurable eons," what are these so-called difficult deeds?

That is to say, when sentient beings desire to attain liberation through the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), the Bodhisattva feels extreme great suffering on their account; wishing to cause them to turn away from that mind set upon a different vehicle, he manifests various forms and, throughout immeasurable worlds over the course of immeasurable eons, is able to endure diligent suffering and perform various difficult deeds for a long time.

"Regarding the nature of body, speech, and mind that does not retreat in order to deliver others: this means that for the sake of delivering others, although a bodhisattva may undergo diligent suffering in various places for a long time, their nature of the three karmas never experiences retreat or discouragement."
The verse says:
Just as a person fearing four harms guards themselves with diligent vigilance;
so too does the Bodhisattva, fearing the two vehicles, protect their karma in this same way.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the bodhisattva’s skillful means for protecting oneself from karma.
It is like a person who, fearing the four harms, guards themselves with great vigilance. What are these four harms?
First, poisonous substances; second, weapons; third, unwholesome food; fourth, enemies—these are called the four harms.
To guard against them deeply is for the sake of benefiting oneself.

Regarding the statement, "The Bodhisattva’s fear of the two vehicles and protection of karma is likewise," the four harms such as poison serve as metaphors for the various karmic expedients of those of the two vehicles; because the Bodhisattva fears these, they deeply protect themselves against giving rise to the mind of the two vehicles.

Why is this? Because it severs the seeds of the Mahāyāna; because it prevents the arising of Mahāyāna roots of goodness that have not yet arisen; because it causes those already arisen to perish; and because it creates obstacles to the fruit of Buddhahood.
The verse says:
When the agent, the action, and the object are not discriminated as three wheels, one crosses the ocean of pure karma; such merit is boundless.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding pure karma.
Regarding the non-differentiation of the three spheres—the agent, the action, and that which is acted upon—what are these three spheres?
First is the agent, second is the action, and third is that which is produced; these are called the three wheels.
One who does not engage in conceptual discrimination is so because these three cannot be apprehended.
By means of this, the three spheres (trimaṇḍala) attain purity; because the three spheres are pure, karma is pure.
Regarding the attainment of boundless merit in crossing the ocean of pure karma: it is because one has reached the further shore of karma.
"Merit is boundless" because it is inexhaustible.
This concludes the Chapter on the Companions of Karma (Karmasahāya).
**Chapter Seventeen: On the Compendium of the Perfections (Pāramitāsaṃgraha), Part One.** Commentary: [The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* states:]
The expedient means for initiating activity have already been explained; now, the perfections (pāramitās) accumulated through that activity shall be discussed.
Herein, first, the summary verse (udāna-gāthā) is stated: [Verse:]
The enumeration, characteristics, sequence, names, Cultivation, distinctions, and inclusion,
The remedies for obstacles, virtues, and mutual manifestation— One should know that these are the ten meanings of the *pāramitās*.
Commentary:
Regarding these six pāramitās, one should know that they possess ten meanings:

first, the establishment of their number; second, the manifestation of their characteristics; third, their sequential order; fourth, the explanation of their names; fifth, their cultivation; sixth, their differentiation; seventh, their inclusion of practices; eighth, their remediation of obstacles; ninth, their merits; and tenth, their mutual illumination.
In this regard, there are six verses establishing that the number of pāramitās is exactly six.
The verse says:
“Requisites, body, retinue, and The arousal [of bodhicitta]—the first four are established.”
The fifth is non-defilement; the sixth is non-perversion.
The commentary states:

This verse demonstrates that the number of pāramitās is established as exactly six for the sake of encompassing three types of self-benefit: first, progress; second, non-defilement; and third, non-perversion.
Those first four pāramitās can cause four matters to progress respectively:
first, the accomplishment of the means of subsistence, by means of generosity;
second, the accomplishment of one's own person, by means of ethical discipline.
Third is the accomplishment of retinue, which results from patience, because those who practice patience are beloved by many people.
Fourth is the accomplishment of undertaking, which results from diligence, because all undertakings are accomplished on its basis.
The fifth is the dhyāna-pāramitā, which enables one to remain unstained by afflictions (*kleśa*), for it is by this power that afflictions are subdued.
The sixth is the prajñā-pāramitā, which ensures that karma is not inverted, because all actions are known according to reality.
The verse says:
Giving to others and not causing them harm, Enduring harm—these are for the benefit of others;
Possessing the causes and abiding in the mind, And liberation—these are for one's own benefit.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates that the number of *pāramitās* is established as exactly six in order to encompass the six matters pertaining to the two benefits.
First, three *pāramitās* are established to encompass the three matters pertaining to the benefit of others, thereby inciting the application of right effort.
In their respective order: first, giving to others; second, not causing them distress; and third, enduring their distress.
Subsequently, for the sake of encompassing the three matters of self-benefit, it is necessary to establish the latter three pāramitās to incite right effort (samyak-vyāyāma).
In their respective order: first, there is the cause, because it relies upon diligence;
second, the abiding of the mind, because it brings the unsettled mind to stability;
third, liberation, because it brings the stabilized mind to liberation.
The verse says:
Without lack and without vexation, enduring affliction and not regressing,
through devotion and skillful speech, benefiting others is itself self-benefit.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates that the number of *pāramitās* is established as exactly six in order to encompass the six types of activities for the benefit of others.

When a bodhisattva practices the six *pāramitās*, they act respectively to ensure that the enjoyments of others are not lacking, to avoid causing them distress, to endure their infliction of harm, to assist them in their undertakings so that they do not regress, to cause them to turn toward the path through the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), and to sever their doubts by means of skillful teaching.

For a bodhisattva, benefiting others in this way is precisely self-benefit; what is done for others is what is done for oneself, because by these causes and conditions one attains great enlightenment.
The verse says:
Non-attachment and supreme reverence, non-retrogression in two ways,
and likewise two kinds of non-conceptuality— these fully encompass the causes of the Mahāyāna.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates that the number of pāramitās is established as exactly six in order to encompass the four causes of the Mahāyāna.
These are: first, non-attachment; second, supreme reverence; third, non-retrogression; and fourth, non-conceptuality.
When a bodhisattva practices generosity, they are unstained by material wealth because they lack attachment to it.
When they uphold the precepts, they give rise to the utmost reverence for all points of training.
When they practice patience and diligence, these two do not regress; for through patience, they do not regress even when encountering suffering inflicted by sentient beings or non-sentient things.
Because one does not regress when practicing virtue with diligence;
and because when practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), these two are non-dual, being subsumed within the equality of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
These four causes encompass all the causes of the Mahāyāna in their entirety.
The verse says:
Non-attachment and non-distraction, non-abandonment and progressive advancement.
Purifying the afflictions and the cognitive obstructions— All paths are entirely subsumed within these.
Commentary:
This verse demonstrates that because the six paths of the Mahāyāna are to be subsumed, the number of *pāramitās* is established as exactly six.
Question:
What is the meaning of "the Path" (mārga)?
Answer:
Skillful means constitute the path.

In this context, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) constitutes the path by way of non-attachment to all material resources, because at the time of giving, one is free from defiled attachment toward the object.
The *śīlapāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline) constitutes the path by means of non-distraction amidst all sensory objects;

for when one seeks to receive the precepts, it gathers and stabilizes all mental distraction, and because when a bhikṣu abides in protection, no confusion of karma can turn him away even when he encounters sensory objects.
The perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) takes non-abandonment of all sentient beings as its path, because it does not give rise to weariness despite any harmful actions.
The perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*) takes the increase of cultivated virtues as its path, because it causes them to flourish through the arousal of diligence.
The dhyāna-pāramitā serves as the path for purifying the afflictive hindrances;
the prajñā-pāramitā serves as the path for purifying the cognitive hindrances.
These six kinds of paths encompass all paths of the Mahāyāna entirely.
The verse says:
In order to encompass the three trainings, it is taught that there are six perfections.
Three, one, two; one, three, two, one, two.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates that the number of pāramitās is established as exactly six in order to encompass the three types of higher training (adhiśikṣā).
Among these, the first three pāramitās are established to encompass the first of the three trainings, namely the training in higher ethical discipline (śīla-adhiśikṣā).
Ethical discipline is of two kinds: the aggregate and its retinue.
Śīla constitutes the aggregate, while dāna and kṣānti constitute the retinue.

Why is this? Because when giving, one is not stingy with material wealth at the time of seeking and receiving; and when practicing patience, one does not retaliate against beatings or insults at the time of protection and maintenance.
Herein, the latter two pāramitās are established in their respective order to encompass the two higher trainings of mind and wisdom.
In this context, it should be understood that the fourth pāramitā fully encompasses the three higher trainings (*adhiśikṣā*), because all three trainings have diligence as their companion.
Having already established the number of the six pāramitās, the characteristics of the six pāramitās are next revealed.
The verse says:
"The essence of the six perfections is analyzed; each one possesses four characteristics."
"Overcoming obstacles, uniting with wisdom, Fulfilling vows, and maturing sentient beings.
The commentary states:
When Bodhisattvas cultivate the various pāramitās, each possesses four aspects:
First, the remediation of obstacles; second, the integration of wisdom; third, the fulfillment of vows; and fourth, the maturation of sentient beings.

Regarding the remediation of obstacles: the six practices beginning with giving (*dāna*) counteract, respectively, stinginess and greed, breaking the precepts, anger, laziness, distracted mind, and delusion.

Regarding "conjoined with wisdom," it means that all [perfections] proceed together with non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), because one has realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Regarding "fulfilling vows": for those seeking wealth, one gives according to their desires; for those seeking ethical discipline (*śīla*), one protects and instructs them through body, speech, and mind according to their desires; for those who repent, one grants joy; for those engaged in diligent effort (*vīrya*), one assists them according to their needs; for those training in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one imparts the Dharma according to their needs; and for those who have doubts, one resolves them according to their needs.
Regarding the maturing of sentient beings: first, one gathers them through generosity, and subsequently matures them according to their respective needs by means of the three vehicles.
First, one establishes them within the precepts and so forth, and subsequently matures them through the three vehicles; it is likewise in this manner.
Having already clarified the characteristics of the six pāramitās, the sequence of the six pāramitās is now explained.
The verse says:
"Prior and posterior, lower and higher, Coarse and subtle—thus they arise in succession."
Thus it is said that there are three causes for the non-disorder [of the sequence] of the six perfections.
The commentary states:
There are three causal conditions for the sequential order of the six *pāramitās*: first, anteriority and posteriority; second, inferiority and superiority; and third, coarseness and subtlety.
Regarding "preceding and succeeding," this means that based on what precedes, what follows can arise.

Why is this? Because one upholds the precepts by disregarding material wealth; having practiced the precepts, one is able to give rise to patience; having practiced patience, one is able to give rise to diligence; having practiced diligence, one is able to give rise to meditative concentration; and having practiced meditative concentration, one is able to understand the true Dharma.
Regarding "lower and higher": that which precedes is the lower and that which follows is the higher.
The lower refers to giving (*dāna*), the higher to ethical discipline (*śīla*); and so on, up to the lower being meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the higher being wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the coarse and the subtle: the former is coarse and the latter is subtle.
The coarse is giving and the subtle is ethical discipline; this continues up to the coarse being meditative concentration and the subtle being wisdom.
Why? Because they are coarse, easy to enter, and easy to practice. Why?
Because they are subtle, difficult to enter, and difficult to practice.
Having already explained the sequence of the six pāramitās, I shall next explain the names of the six pāramitās.
The verse says:
Removing poverty and bringing coolness, Destroying anger and establishing virtue,
Mental retention and true understanding— These are explained as the meaning of the six practices.
The commentary states:
It is called "giving" (dāna) because it can eliminate poverty;
it is called "precept" (śīla) because it can bring about coolness, for in one who possesses the precepts, the fever of afflictions subsides amidst the appearances of sensory objects.
It is called patience (*kṣānti*) because it can destroy ill-will; for through patience, one destroys ill-will and brings it to exhaustion.
It is called diligence (*vīrya*) because it can establish the wholesome; for it is by this power that wholesome dharmas are established.
It is called concentration (*samādhi*) because it is able to sustain the mind, thereby gathering and holding the internal faculty of thought.
It is called wisdom (*prajñā*) because it is able to discern the true Dharma, thereby clearly understanding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Having explained the names of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), I shall next discuss the cultivation of the six perfections.
The verse says:
Regarding objects, reflection, and the mind, As well as skillful means and power,
one should know that the cultivation of the six practices Is said to have five bases of reliance.
The commentary states:

There are five bases for the cultivation of the various pāramitās by bodhisattvas: first, the basis of material things; second, the basis of reflection; third, the basis of the mind; fourth, the basis of skillful means; and fifth, the basis of power.
There are four kinds of reliance for practicing the various pāramitās:
first, reliance on the cause, because one practices by relying on the power of the spiritual lineage (gotra);
second, reliance on maturation, because one practices by relying on the power of the accomplishment of one's own body.
Third is reliance on aspiration, because one practices by relying on the power of former aspirations.
Fourth is reliance on frequency, because one practices by relying on the power of wisdom.
There are also four kinds of contemplation based on which one cultivates the various pāramitās:
first, contemplation through faith, because one generates faith toward the teachings associated with the pāramitās.
Second is the contemplation of savoring, because one perceives the flavor of merit within all the pāramitās.
Third is the contemplation of sympathetic joy, because one gives rise to sympathetic joy toward all the pāramitās practiced by all sentient beings in all worlds.
Fourth is the contemplation of aspiration, because one arouses aspiration for all superior perfections (pāramitās) that will belong to oneself and others in the future.
There are six kinds of mental reliance when practicing the various perfections:
first, the tireless mind; second, the vast mind; third, the mind of supreme joy; fourth, the mind of great benefit; fifth, the unstained mind; and sixth, the well-purified mind.
What are the six kinds of mind in the cultivation of *dāna*?

If a bodhisattva, with the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and even with his own life, were to give to a single sentient being in a single kṣaṇa, and continue in this manner until all the realms of sentient beings are exhausted.
Regarding the maturation of one's vow for unsurpassed bodhi, the mind of giving through this gateway is never satiated; such a mental state is called the "insatiable mind in the cultivation of dāna."

If a bodhisattva practices giving with such characteristics, from its initial continuity until the attainment of Buddhahood, there is not even for a single moment any interruption or diminution; such a mental state is called the vast mind that cultivates *dāna*.

If a bodhisattva, when gathering others through giving, gives rise to an extremely profound joy that exceeds the joy felt by the recipient upon obtaining wealth, such a state of mind is called the superior joyful mind of practicing *dāna*.

When a bodhisattva gathers others through giving, they perceive that the other person’s receiving of the gift is of the greatest benefit to themselves, rather than their own personal use being of the greatest benefit. Why is this?

Because gathering others through giving serves as the cause for my own accomplishment of unsurpassed bodhi, a mind characterized in this way is called the "mind that cultivates the excellence of dāna.
If a bodhisattva practices such extensive giving without seeking gratitude or karmic retribution, a mind characterized in this way is called the "mind that cultivates dāna without defilement."

If a bodhisattva practices such extensive giving, they dedicate the mass of merit and the resulting karmic fruit to all sentient beings rather than for their own enjoyment; furthermore, sharing it with all sentient beings, they dedicate it toward unexcelled enlightenment. Such a mental state is called the pure mind that cultivates the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
What are the six kinds of mind regarding the cultivation of precepts?

Suppose a bodhisattva possesses as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and each body has a lifespan of as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; within each lifespan, they lack all necessities of life, and amidst this deprivation, a mass of fire fills the entirety of a trichiliocosm.

With these many bodies, throughout these many lifetimes, and within this mass of fire, the bodhisattva maintains the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), yet in a single moment cultivates only a single precept.

In this manner, until all the aggregates of precepts are exhausted, and even until all the aggregates of wisdom are exhausted, the bodhisattva practices with a mind that never tires of attaining unsurpassed enlightenment. Such a mental state is called the "insatiable mind in the cultivation of the precepts and so forth."

If a bodhisattva, from the initial cultivation of ethical discipline up to the cultivation of wisdom, remains seated at the site of enlightenment without interruption, such a mental state is called the vast mind that cultivates ethical discipline and the other perfections.

When a bodhisattva cultivates the perfections such as ethical discipline to gather others, they give rise to an extremely profound joy that exceeds the joy felt by those being gathered when they receive benefit; a mind characterized in this way is called the "mind of superior joy" in cultivating ethical discipline and the other perfections.

When a bodhisattva cultivates the perfections such as ethical discipline (*śīla*) to gather others, they perceive that the benefit received by others is an extreme benefit to themselves; they do not regard their own self-interest as the supreme benefit. Such a mental state is called the mind that cultivates the excellence of ethical discipline and the other perfections.

When a bodhisattva practices the precepts and so forth, if they do not seek gratitude or karmic retribution, such a state of mind is called the "unstained mind" in practicing the precepts and so forth.

If a bodhisattva, regarding the fruit of retribution resulting from the vast cultivation of the merit of the precepts and so forth, vows to bestow it upon all sentient beings rather than receiving it themselves, and further shares it with all sentient beings, dedicating it toward unsurpassed enlightenment—such a mental state is called the pure and virtuous mind that cultivates the precepts and so forth.

There are three kinds of reliance on skillful means for cultivating the various *pāramitās*; these three kinds are precisely the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddhi*), and this purity arises because non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*) serves as the skillful means.
By means of these skillful methods, all mental engagements are fully accomplished.
There are also three kinds of power upon which the cultivation of the perfections relies: first, the power of the body; second, the power of practice; and third, the power of teaching.
The power of the body (*kāya-vaśitā*) should be understood as the Buddha’s *svābhāvika-kāya* (essential body) and *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body).

The power of conduct (*caryā-vaśitā*) should be understood as the Buddha’s *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body), because by means of this emanation body, he manifests all virtuous deeds for all sentient beings in all their various forms.
Regarding the explanation of "power" (*bala*): it refers to the absence of obstruction when expounding all aspects of the six *pāramitās*.
*Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*, Fascicle Seven;

Part Two of the Seventeenth Chapter, "The Compendium of the Two Degrees. The commentary states:
Having already explained the cultivation of the six pāramitās, I shall next explain the distinctions among the six pāramitās.
Each of the distinctions of the six pāramitās has six meanings:
first, essential nature; second, cause; third, fruit; fourth, function; fifth, association; and sixth, classification.
The verse says:
Giving to others and the volition associated with it, These two constitute [giving] and are also subsumed by the two;
Because one dwells fully without stinginess, There are three types: dharma, wealth, and fearlessness.
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies the six meanings of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
"Giving to others" constitutes the essential nature of giving, because one bestows one's own possessions upon various recipients.
Volition (cetanā) is the cause of giving, because it arises simultaneously with the wholesome root of non-attachment.
The two accomplishments are the fruits of giving, because they consist of the accomplishment of wealth and the accomplishment of the body.
Regarding the accomplishment of the body, it fully encompasses five matters, such as those described in the *Pañcavastuka-sūtra*:
"By giving food, one obtains five things: first, life; second, beauty; third, strength; fourth, happiness; and fifth, eloquence."
The two types of gathering are the activity of giving, because they fulfill the gathering of both oneself and others, as well as the fulfillment of great enlightenment.
"Abiding fully in non-avarice" refers to its association with giving, because it abides fully within the minds of those who possess non-avarice.
The three—Dharma, wealth, and fearlessness—are the categories of giving.
There are three categories because there is:
first, the gift of Dharma; second, the gift of wealth; and third, the gift of fearlessness.
These six points are what the wise should know and practice.
The verse says:
The six branches, the cessation of existence, the limit, The wholesome path, and the upholding, etc.
"Because of the perfection of the accumulation of merit, the two attainments are of two kinds.
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies the six meanings of the *śīlapāramitā*.
The six limbs are the intrinsic nature of the precepts, because one abides in the complete observance of the precepts and even trains in the various branches of training.

"Destroying the limits of existence" is the cause of the precepts; "destruction" refers to nirvana, for one receives and practices the precepts in order to seek nirvana and transcend the limits of all forms of existence.
The "good path" (sugati) is the fruit of morality; it refers to the successive states of mind, such as the good path and freedom from regret, which are attained because they are caused by morality.
"Maintaining [the precepts]" and so forth constitute the activity of morality.
Precepts possess three capacities:
first, the capacity to uphold, because they can sustain all meritorious qualities like the great earth;
second, the capacity to pacify, because they can extinguish the feverish heat of all afflictions.

Third is fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*): because one is able to refrain from giving rise to the causal conditions for all transgressions, such as fear and hatred, how could one fear the arising of such transgressions?

"Being fully endowed with a mass of merit" refers to its correspondence with ethical discipline (*śīla*), because at all times the actions of body, speech, and mind are practiced as wholesome conduct.
Regarding "the two acquisitions constitute two types," this refers to the categories of the precepts (*śīla*).
The two acquisitions are the acquisition through undertaking (*samādāna-labdha*) and the acquisition through the Dharma (*dharma-labdha*).
Acquisition through undertaking comprises the *prātimokṣa* restraint (*saṃvara*).
Regarding the attainment of the Dharma, it comprises the protection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the outflow-free protection (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
The verse says:
The nature of non-retaliation, endurance, and wisdom, Great compassion, and reliance upon the Dharma.
The five virtues together with the two benefits, Possessing these, they excel those three kinds.
Commentary:
This verse clarifies the six meanings of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Non-retaliation, endurance, and wisdom constitute the intrinsic nature of patience (*kṣānti*).
First, non-retaliation; second, endurance; third, wisdom—these three, in this sequence, are the intrinsic natures of the three types of patience.

Not retaliating is the intrinsic nature of patience toward injury by others; enduring is the intrinsic nature of patience toward suffering; and wisdom is the intrinsic nature of patience through the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmāḥ*).
Great compassion and reliance upon the Dharma are the causes of patience: first, great compassion as the cause, and second, reliance upon the Dharma as the cause.
The basis of the Dharma refers to receiving the precepts and possessing extensive learning.
The five virtues are the fruits of patience; as stated in the sūtras, patience yields five kinds of fruits: first, one incurs little hatred or resentment;

second, one does not cause others' minds to become corrupted; third, one attains joy and happiness; fourth, one has no regrets at the time of death; and fifth, upon the dissolution of the body, one is reborn in heaven.
The "two benefits" refer to the activity of patience; through the three types of patience, one is able to perform the two kinds of activities for the benefit of oneself and others.
As a verse in a sutra says:
"To accomplish those two purposes—benefiting oneself and benefiting others—if one knows that another is angry, one should personally cease [the anger] toward them."

"Endowed with the supreme" means being associated with patience (*kṣānti*). Because patience is difficult to practice, it is called "supreme"; to be fully endowed with this supremacy is what is meant by "associated.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Patience is the highest, because it is difficult to practice."
Those three types constitute the category of patience (*kṣānti*).

That person possesses three grades because there is: first, patience toward being reviled by others; second, patience toward enduring suffering; and third, patience through the contemplation of dharmas.
The verse says:
In regard to the wholesome and the correct, through diligence, Because of having faith and aspiration,
Through the increase of mindfulness and the application of remedies, These seven possess such virtues.
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies the six meanings of the *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of vigor).

Regarding "the heroism toward the wholesome and the correct": this refers to the intrinsic nature of vigor. It is called "wholesome" because it excludes heroism directed toward other [worldly] activities; it is called "correct" because it excludes heroism directed toward the liberation [proclaimed by] non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The presence of faith and aspiration is the cause of diligence, because diligence arises through faith and the pursuit of it.
The increase of mindfulness is the fruit of diligence, because qualities such as mindfulness and concentration arise further from diligence.
As for the remedy, this is the activity of diligence; as it is said in the Sūtra:
"One who arouses diligence is able to dwell in happiness, because they are not mixed with various evil and unwholesome dharmas."
"Endowed with virtue" means being associated with diligence, because of possessing virtues such as non-attachment and so forth.
"Those seven types" refers to the categories of diligence; that person possesses seven kinds of diligence:

first, diligence in training in ethical discipline (*śīla*); second, diligence in training in meditative concentration (*samādhi*); third, diligence in training in wisdom (*prajñā*); fourth, physical diligence; fifth, mental diligence; sixth, uninterrupted diligence; and seventh, respectful diligence.
The verse says:
Abiding of mind, mindfulness, and exertion, Arising of joy, as well as concentration and abiding— These are the foremost among all dharmas;
Their seeds are threefold, and again threefold.
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies the six meanings of the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā).
"The mind abides" refers to the intrinsic nature of meditative concentration, because the mind abides within.
Mindfulness and exertion are the causes of concentration: because of mindfulness, one does not forget the object; because of exertion, meditative concentration can arise.
The arising of joy is the fruit of concentration, for it is free from the means of retrogression and its fruit is never in vain.
Regarding "pervasive abiding" (*sāmānyavihāra*), this is a determinate karma. "Pervasive" refers to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*); "abiding" refers to the three abidings:

the noble abiding (*āryavihāra*), the celestial abiding (*divyavihāra*), and the Brahma abiding (*brahmavihāra*). This is because meditative concentration (*dhyānasamādhi*) enables one to attain mastery and abide in both the five supernormal powers and the three abidings.
That which is the foremost of all dharmas is associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as it is said in the Sūtra:
"Because *samādhi* is the foremost of all dharmas.
Regarding the phrase "those three types, each again being three," these are the categories of concentration; such a person possesses two kinds of threefold categories.
First, because there are three categories: with vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka but with vicāra, and without vitarka and without vicāra;
second, because there are three categories: accompanied by joy, accompanied by bliss, and accompanied by equanimity.
The verse says:
Right discernment, meditative concentration, and retention;
excellent liberation and the teaching on life—these are the foremost among all dharmas, and each of them also has three types.
The commentary states:
This verse clarifies the six meanings of *prajñāpāramitā*.

"Correct discernment" (*samyak-pravicaya*) is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of wisdom (*prajñā*), because it correctly discerns supramundane phenomena by way of abandoning erroneous activities and those activities known in the world.
Concentration as maintenance is the cause of wisdom, because by maintaining wisdom through concentration, one understands phenomena as they truly are.
Skillful liberation is the fruit of wisdom, meaning that one attains skillful liberation from defilements.
Why is this? It is because of the correct discernment (*samyak-pravicaya*) that is mundane, supramundane, and greatly supramundane.
To say "one whose life is speech" refers to the activity of wisdom; for one whose life is wisdom and who speaks well of the life of wisdom takes that unsurpassed correct discernment as their life.
One who speaks well does so because they correctly expound the true Dharma.
Being the foremost among all dharmas means being associated with wisdom, as it is said in the sūtras:
"Prajñā is the supreme among all dharmas."
"That which also has three kinds" refers to the categories of wisdom; for such a person possesses the three types of correct discernment: mundane, supramundane, and great supramundane.
Having explained the distinctions among the six pāramitās, the practice of subsuming them [within one another] will now be discussed.
The verse says:
One should know that all pure and wholesome dharmas Are comprised of both the distracted and the concentrated.
The six perfections comprise three pairs; all such categories are fully subsumed within them.
The commentary states:
"All pure and white dharmas" refers to the various practices of dharma, such as *dāna* (generosity) and the rest.
It should be understood that these practices of the Dharma are subsumed under three categories:
first, distraction; second, concentration; and third, both.
Regarding distraction, it is because the first two pāramitās—generosity and ethical discipline—are not fixed in concentration.
"Concentration" refers to the fact that the latter two pāramitās encompass both meditative absorption (dhyāna) and the concentration of true wisdom (prajñā).
"Both together" refers to the fact that the middle two pāramitās encompass both patience (kṣānti) and diligence (vīrya), as well as concentration and non-concentration.
Having already explained the practice as subsumed by the six pāramitās, next the treatment of their obstacles is explained.
The verse says:
Because generosity is free from seven attachments, seven types of non-attachment are taught.
One should know that for the remaining five perfections, the seven obstacles and their remedies are likewise so.
The commentary states:
Because giving is free from the seven attachments, it is said to be "non-attachment. As for those seven kinds of attachment to giving: [text follows]

First, attachment to material wealth; second, attachment to laxity; third, attachment to biased adherence; fourth, attachment to requiting gratitude; fifth, attachment to karmic retribution; sixth, attachment to obstacles; and seventh, attachment to distraction.
Among these, "attachment due to obstruction" refers to the failure to sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of greed, which are the specific objects to be countered by generosity (*dāna*).
Regarding "attachment due to distraction," there are two kinds of distraction:
first, distraction of inferior intent, because of seeking the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); [and second, distraction of external objects, because of being drawn toward sensory pleasures].
Second is the distraction of conceptualization, because one conceptualizes the three spheres.
Since a bodhisattva, when practicing generosity, remains far removed from these seven attachments, the "seven non-attachments" are taught.

Regarding the statement, "One should know that for the remaining five perfections, the seven obstacles and their remedies are likewise so": one should understand that the five pāramitās, beginning with ethical discipline (*śīla*), each also have seven attachments; because they are free from these seven attachments, seven forms of non-attachment are likewise taught for each.

In this context, there is a distinction: the reversal of attachment to material resources through the *dāna-pāramitā* is precisely the detachment from the "primary" attachments associated with the other five *pāramitās*. That is to say: morality (*śīla*) is detachment from attachment to breaking the precepts; patience (*kṣānti*) is detachment from attachment to malice; diligence (*vīrya*) is detachment from attachment to laziness; meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is detachment from attachment to a distracted mind; and wisdom (*prajñā*) is detachment from attachment to ignorance.
Regarding "precepts and so forth being free from the attachment of hindrances": this is because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of those hindrances have all been eliminated.
Regarding "precepts and so forth being free from the attachment of conceptualization": this is because one does not conceptualize the three spheres (*trimandala*).
Having already explained the remedies for the obstacles to the six perfections, the merits of the six perfections will now be discussed.
Within this, the merit of benefiting others is explained first.
The verse says:
Constantly relinquishing body and life, Free from seeking and out of compassion for others, One establishes bodhi through giving;
Wisdom encompasses this inexhaustible giving.
Commentary:
This verse demonstrates the merit of benefiting others through the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
"Constantly relinquishing body and life" means that bodhisattvas at all times bestow their own bodies and lives upon all who seek them.
"Being free from seeking because of compassion for others" means not seeking recompense or the fruits of affection, as great compassion serves as the cause.
"Establishing enlightenment through giving" means that, having practiced this giving, one establishes all sentient beings in the enlightenment of the three vehicles.

Regarding "giving embraced by wisdom is inexhaustible": this giving is embraced by non-conceptual wisdom; its merit remains inexhaustible until even the nirvana without remainder, because it provides infinite benefit to all sentient beings.
The verse says:
Constantly guarding the prohibitions with diligence, Transcending both the precepts and the happy realms,
Taking the precepts as the cause for establishing bodhi, Wisdom encompasses the precepts so they are inexhaustible.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the merit of benefiting others through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).

Regarding "the diligent one who constantly observes the prohibitions," the bodhisattva possesses the threefold aggregate of ethical discipline (*trividhaṃ śīlaskandham*): [the discipline of restraint, the discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the discipline of benefiting sentient beings].

The first is the vow of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the second is the vow of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the third is the vow of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*).
The first vow has the nature of prohibition and prevention, while the latter two vows have the nature of diligent effort, because Bodhisattvas constantly guard them at all times.
"Detached from the precepts and the happy realms" means that one does not cling to the attainment of the precepts nor seek their pleasant fruits.
The verse says:
"At all times enduring the insults of others, Free from seeking and the fear of incapacity."
"By means of patience one establishes bodhi; wisdom encompasses patience inexhaustibly.
Commentary:
This verse demonstrates the merit of benefiting others through the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

Regarding "constantly enduring the slanders of others": at all times, even if all sentient beings were to come and revile the bodhisattva with every form of most grievous affliction, the bodhisattva is able to endure it all.
Free from seeking, fear, and inability: one does not seek recompense, nor seek a favorable rebirth, nor act out of fear, nor out of incapacity.
The verse says:
"Always vowing to exert oneself, making the slaying of the thieves supreme."
Because he advances toward enlightenment, his wisdom encompasses inexhaustible progress.
Commentary:
This verse demonstrates the merit of benefiting others through the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
Regarding "vowing to exert oneself diligently at all times," the peerless cultivation of diligence by all bodhisattvas has two essential natures:
first, the vow as its essential nature; second, the diligent application of skillful means as its essential nature.

"Slaying the thieves as supreme" means that a bodhisattva practices diligence solely for the purpose of slaying the thieves of afflictions within themselves and others, in order to attain unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*).
The verse says:
Constantly practicing all meditative concentrations, They relinquish dhyāna and take birth in lower realms.
"Based on meditative concentration, one establishes bodhi; wisdom embraces concentration inexhaustibly.
Commentary:
This verse demonstrates the merit of benefiting others through the perfection of dhyāna (meditative concentration).
"Those who constantly practice all meditative concentrations" refers to the bodhisattvas who cultivate by encompassing infinite samādhis.
"Abandoning dhyāna to be born in lower realms" means that they relinquish dwelling in the unsurpassed bliss of dhyāna and come to take birth in inferior states.
Why is this? It is because of great compassion.
The verse says:
Constantly realizing the truth and other objects, even the Buddha’s cessation does not cling to them;
through causal wisdom he establishes bodhi, and his compassion embraces wisdom without end.
Commentary:
This verse demonstrates the merit of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) in benefiting others.

Regarding the phrase "constantly comprehending reality and other objects": "comprehending reality" refers to the equal characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), because it is the wisdom that realizes the twofold selflessness of persons and phenomena.
