Chapter Twenty-Three: Conduct in Walking and Standing. Commentary:
Having already explained the qualities of a bodhisattva, the five characteristics of a bodhisattva will now be explained.
The verse says:
Possessing compassion within the mind, Affectionate speech, and courageous vigor;
Opening the hand and explaining the meaning—these are the five characteristics of a bodhisattva.
The commentary states:
There are five kinds of characteristics of a bodhisattva: first, compassion; second, kind speech; third, courage; fourth, opening the hand; and fifth, explaining the meaning.
"Compassionate" means gathering and benefiting sentient beings through the bodhicitta.
"Affectionate in speech" means causing them to attain correct faith in the Buddha-dharma.
"Valiant and courageous" means not retreating or being cowed by difficult practices and ascetic austerities.
The "one who opens the hand" gathers [beings] through material wealth;
the "one who explains the meaning" gathers [beings] through the Dharma.
Regarding these five aspects, it should be understood that the first one is the mind and the latter four are conduct.
Having explained the five characteristics of a bodhisattva, the distinction between the householder and the renunciant bodhisattva will now be discussed.
The verse says:
At all times, the bodhisattva Constantly dwells in the position of a wheel-turning monarch.
"Benefiting sentient beings is performed; such is the division for those at home.
The commentary states:

When a bodhisattva is at home, he constantly acts as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), transforming others through the practice of the ten wholesome paths and remaining free from the ten unwholesome paths; this is what constitutes benefiting them.
The verse says:
Through formal reception, through attainment of the Dharma, and through manifestation,
there are three types of renunciation that exist throughout all stages.
The commentary states:
There are three types of ordination for a bodhisattva who leaves the household life. First is the ordination by reception, which refers to receiving the protection from another;
second is the ordination by dharma, which refers to attaining the untainted (anāsrava) protection.
The stage of manifesting [the result] (*saṃdarśana-bhāga*) refers to the attainment of transformation and enjoyment (*nirmāṇa-sambhogika-lābha*).
The stage of attaining the Dharma (*dharma-lābha-bhāga*) and the stage of manifesting [the result] refer to entering the great stages (*mahābhūmi*).
The verse says:
One should know that the portion of the renunciant life, endowed with immeasurable merit,
when compared to the portion of the householder, is supreme and beyond compare.
The commentary states:
When comparing the two categories, the category of those who have gone forth is superior because it is endowed with immeasurable merit.
Having already explained the categories of the bodhisattva’s life at home and the life of going forth, we shall next explain the five kinds of extremely great resolve of a bodhisattva.
The verse says:
Desire for the fruit of love and the roots of goodness, Desiring to attain nirvāṇa,
The impure, the pure, and the utterly pure— These are said to exist within the various stages (*bhūmi*).

The commentary states: The five supreme great minds are: first, the supreme great mind of joy; second, the supreme great mind of benefit; third, the supreme great mind of the unpurified; fourth, the supreme great mind of the purified; and fifth, the supreme great mind of the utterly purified.
The "fruit of affection" refers to the extremely great mind of joy, which causes all sentient beings to obtain the desirable fruits of future lives.
The "root of goodness" refers to the extremely great mind of benefit, which causes all sentient beings to practice various virtues in the present and attain nirvāṇa.
"Those who are not yet purified" refers to those whose supreme great mind is not yet purified, namely bodhisattvas on the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*).
"Those who are purified" refers to those whose supreme great mind has already been purified, namely bodhisattvas from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) up to the seventh stage (*saptamabhūmi*).
"Utmost purity" refers to the utterly pure and vast mind, namely that of Bodhisattvas in the final three stages.
Having explained the five kinds of vast minds of Bodhisattvas, we shall next explain the four kinds of gathering of sentient beings by Bodhisattvas.
The verse says: Through desire for joy, equanimity, Supremacy, and [guiding] the assembly—
These four mentalities, across all stages, Encompass all sentient beings.
The commentary states:
Regarding the four ways of gathering sentient beings: first, gathering through the mind of aspiration, because one gathers them by means of the bodhicitta;
second, gathering through the mind of equality, because upon entering the first stage (bhūmi), one attains the mind of equality between self and others.
Third is inclusion by the mind of superior resolve (*adhiṣṭhāna-citta*), because one includes others through the power of mastery while occupying a position of leadership;
fourth is inclusion by the mind of the retinue (*gaṇa-citta*), because one includes them by making them one's own disciples.
Having already explained the four ways in which Bodhisattvas gather sentient beings, next the four ways in which Bodhisattvas take birth will be explained.
The verse says:
Through the power of karma and the power of vows, Through the power of meditative concentration and the power of supernatural faculties.
Relying upon these four kinds of power, the Bodhisattva undergoes birth.
The commentary states:

regarding the four kinds of birth, first is birth through the power of karma; second is birth through the power of vows; third is birth through the power of meditative concentration; and fourth is birth through the power of supernormal faculties.

Birth through the power of karma refers to Bodhisattvas on the stage of practice through faith (śraddhācaryābhūmi), who possess mastery over the power of karma and thus take birth in whatever place they desire.

Birth through the power of aspiration refers to Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages (mahābhūmi), who possess mastery over the power of aspiration and thus take birth as animals and so forth for the sake of maturing others.

Birth through the power of meditative concentration refers to Bodhisattvas who have attained concentration and possess mastery over its power, such that they relinquish birth in the higher realms to take birth in the lower ones.

Birth through the power of supernormal faculties refers to Bodhisattvas who have attained supernatural powers and possess mastery over their power, being able to manifest various forms within the Tuṣita Heaven and other realms in order to take birth there.
Having already explained the four ways in which Bodhisattvas take birth, next the characteristics of the eleven stages of the Bodhisattva will be explained.
The verse says:
Realizing emptiness and realizing the fruit of karma, Abiding in dhyāna and abiding in the factors of enlightenment.
Contemplating the truths and contemplating dependent origination, Without signs and without effort,
purifying the two gates through the power of transformation, And purifying awakening—
through these various explanations, One should understand the establishment of the stages (bhūmis).
The commentary states:
The "eleven abodes" refers to the eleven stages (*bhūmi*), for an "abode" is termed a "stage.
The phrase "realizing emptiness" reveals the characteristics of the first stage, as one dwells extensively in the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena.
Realizing the fruits of karma reveals the characteristics of the second stage, as one realizes that karma and its fruits are indestructible and is thus able to protect the precepts.
Abiding in dhyāna reveals the characteristics of the third stage, as one is able to be born in the desire realm without falling back from dhyāna.

Abiding in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) reveals the characteristics of the fourth stage, because one is able to enter into birth and death without abandoning the factors of enlightenment.

Contemplating the truths (*satya*) reveals the characteristics of the fifth stage, because it clarifies that afflictions in the process of teaching and transforming others afflict only the mind, as there is no self (*ātman*).

Contemplating dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) reveals the characteristics of the sixth stage, because one is able to take birth in dependence upon dependent origination without giving rise to a defiled mind.
The signless (*animitta*) reveals the characteristics of the seventh stage, because although practice still involves effort, it ascends toward the single path and dwells frequently in the signless.

"Effortlessness" (*anābhoga*) reveals the characteristics of the eighth stage (*vihāra*); although it purifies Buddha-fields, there is no deliberate activity, because one dwells predominantly in effortlessness.

"Power of transformation" (*nirmāṇa-vaśitā*) reveals the characteristics of the ninth stage; through mastery of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one is able to bring all sentient beings to maturity.
The purification of the two gates reveals the characteristics of the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), because the gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī are utterly pure.
The purification of bodhi reveals the characteristics of the eleventh stage, because the obstructions to omniscience (*sarvajñāvaraṇa*) have been completely severed.
The characteristics of the eleven stages of a bodhisattva have already been explained; next, the establishment of names for these stages based on the grounds (*bhūmi*) will be discussed.
The verse says:
"The first three purify the three types of conduct; the next three sever the three types of pride."
"The last three are awakening, relinquishing, and transforming; the tenth has four names.
The commentary states:
Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), ten names for bodhisattvas are established.

Regarding the purification through three practices in the first three stages: in the first stage (*bhūmi*), there is "purification of view," because the bodhisattva attains the wisdom that serves as the antidote to the two views of self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*).
In the second stage, there is "purification of ethical discipline" (*śīla-viśuddhi*), because even the subtlest stains of transgression have no substance whatsoever for the bodhisattva.
The third stage is called "Purity of Concentration" (*samādhi-viśuddhi*), because the bodhisattva attains non-retrogression in all dhyānas and samādhis.

Regarding the subsequent elimination of the three types of pride: on the fourth stage, one eliminates the pride of diversity regarding the gateways to the Dharma (*dharma-mukha-nānātva-māna*), because the bodhisattva destroys the arising of pride concerning distinctions among the various sūtras and teachings.
The fifth stage is called "Severing the Pride of Diversity in the Continuum," because the bodhisattva enters the ten kinds of equanimous mind and thereby attains equanimity toward all continua.

The sixth stage is called "Severing the Pride of Diversity between Defilement and Purity," because the bodhisattva, like the nature which is fundamentally pure yet defiled by adventitious dust, is able to abide in the dharma of dependent origination without giving rise to views that differentiate between black and white.

Regarding the "subsequent three awakenings that relinquish transformation": on the seventh stage, one attains awakening; because the Bodhisattva dwells in the power of signlessness (*animitta*), they are able to cultivate the thirty-seven factors of awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*) in every moment of thought.
The eighth stage is called the Stage of Equanimity (*upekṣā*), because the bodhisattva dwells in effortless (*anābhoga*) signlessness (*animitta*);
it is also called the Pure Land (*śuddhakṣetra*), because the bodhisattva’s skillful practice merges with that of bodhisattvas on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
The ninth stage is called "Maturing Sentient Beings," because the bodhisattva is able to bring all sentient beings to maturity.
The tenth stage has four names: first, "Great Supernatural Power," because the bodhisattva attains great supernatural powers;
second, "Fulfilling the Dharma-body," because the bodhisattva is endowed with immeasurable gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī.
Third is the manifestation of the body, because the Bodhisattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven and so forth, manifesting the form-body;
fourth is the reception of office, because the Bodhisattva receives his office from all the Buddhas.
Having explained how the names of the bodhisattvas are established based on the stages (*bhūmi*), next the training according to each stage and the fruit of that training will be explained.
The verse says:
"Following the sequence, relying on the first six [stages], One realizes the nature of reality and cultivates the three trainings."
"In succession, based on the latter four, there are four kinds of attainment of the fruit.
The commentary explains:

"In succession, based on the former six, regarding the nature of vision and the cultivation of the three trainings," this means that a bodhisattva penetrates *tathatā* (suchness) in the first stage (*bhūmi*); in the second stage, they train in higher morality (*adhiśīla*); in the third stage, they train in higher mind (*adhicitta*); and in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, they train in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
Wisdom has two objects: first, the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*), namely the Four Noble Truths such as suffering;
second, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), namely the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order.
These two objects also exist in the second and third stages; therefore, those stages are likewise established as having superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).

However, in the fourth stage, the wisdom of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) is predominant; in the fifth stage, the wisdom of discerning the truths (*satya*) is predominant; and in the sixth stage, the wisdom of contemplating dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is predominant. Therefore, the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) is established across these three stages.
Regarding the four kinds of fruits obtained sequentially based on the latter four [stages]: based on the seventh stage, one attains the dwelling in signlessness with effort, which is the first fruit.
Based on the eighth stage, one attains the dwelling in signlessness without effort, which is the second fruit.
Relying on the ninth stage, one attains the maturation of sentient beings; this constitutes the third fruit.
Relying on the tenth stage, one attains maturation through two gates; this constitutes the fourth fruit.

Having already explained the training according to the stages and the fruits of that training, next we shall explain the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) according to the stages.
The verse says:
"Seeing the nature, the purity, and the three bodies, Also occur within the first six stages."
The remaining stages purify the other two, because they are far removed from the five obstacles.
The commentary states:

The realization of the nature [of reality] in the first stage is as explained previously; in the second stage, the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*) is purified; in the third stage, the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*) is purified; and in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*) is purified.
In the final four stages and the Buddha stage, the body of liberation and the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation are purified because of the abandonment of the five obstacles.

As for these five obstacles: in the seventh stage, ignorance regarding the grasping of signs constitutes an obstacle; in the eighth stage, ignorance regarding effortful application constitutes an obstacle; in the ninth stage, ignorance regarding the inability to manifest births through transformation constitutes an obstacle; and in the tenth stage, ignorance regarding the two gates that have not yet been purified constitutes an obstacle.

In the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*), the obstacle consists of ignorance that acts as a hindrance; that is to say, this ignorance can obstruct the wisdom regarding the spheres of experience of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Because the Buddhas know all objects without obstruction, they have attained liberation from this obstacle.

Having explained how Bodhisattvas cultivate the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-skandha) according to each stage (bhūmi), next the accomplishment and non-accomplishment of these stages by Bodhisattvas will be explained.
The verse says:
Non-achievement and achievement, Achievement followed by non-achievement and achievement.
"Establishing knowledge as the earth, / Distinguishing and non-distinguishing.
Commentary:
Regarding "the unaccomplished and the accomplished": the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*) is the unaccomplished, while all the remaining stages are called the accomplished.

Regarding "accomplished yet not accomplished, and accomplished": within the aforementioned stages of accomplishment, there is further that which is not yet accomplished and that which is accomplished; those from the seventh stage downward are termed "not yet accomplished" because they involve effortful application (*sābhoga*).
From the eighth stage upward is called "accomplishment" (niṣpanna), because it is characterized by effortlessness (anābhoga).
Question:
It was previously stated that the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) is also accomplishment; how is this to be understood?
Answer:

As for the establishment of the stages (*bhūmi*), one knows both the conceptualized and the non-conceptualized. This means that within the establishment of the stages, one knows that there is only conceptualization; yet even regarding this conceptualization, there is no conceptualization, because both the grasped object and the grasping subject lack any intrinsic nature. It is with reference to this meaning that it is said to be "accomplished" (*siddha*).
The verse says:
One should know that within the various stages, both cultivation and accomplishment are inconceivable, for they are the domain of the Buddhas.
The commentary states:

Regarding the various stages (*bhūmi*), each has its own cultivation and realization; one should know that every stage is inconceivable, because these are realized through the internal self-awakening of the Bodhisattvas and are known by the Buddhas alone, being beyond the sphere of other persons.
Having already explained the attainment and non-attainment of the bodhisattva according to the stages, next are explained the ten characteristics of a bodhisattva entering the stages.
The verse says:
Clear faith and lack of inferiority, Absence of timidity and absence of dependence.
Thorough penetration and equanimity, Freedom from partiality and freedom from attachment,
As well as knowledge of skillful means— These ten characteristics are present in noble beings,
And are fully perfected in each and every stage.
The commentary states:
For a Bodhisattva who has entered the stages, each stage possesses ten characteristics. What are these ten?

1. Clear faith; 2. absence of inferiority; 3. absence of timidity; 4. absence of dependence; 5. thorough penetration; 6. equanimity; 7. freedom from partiality; 8. freedom from attachment; 9. knowledge of skillful means; 10. being a noble sentient being.
"Clear understanding" means attaining clarity regarding one's own stage, because it eliminates ignorance concerning all phenomena;
"faith" means attaining faith regarding other stages, because it gives rise to aspiration and delight for the subsequent stages.
They are "without inferiority" because they are not startled or terrified upon hearing the profound and subtle Dharma.
They are "without timidity" because they are extremely courageous in practicing what is difficult to practice.
They are "without dependence" because they initiate practices of their own stage without depending on instruction.
"Thorough penetration" means that one is able to give rise to the skillful means of other stages.
"Equanimity" means that toward all sentient beings, one regards them as identical to one's own mind.
"Freedom from partiality" means that upon hearing praise or blame with the ears, there is no sense of superiority or inferiority.
"Free from attachment" means that one attains the rank of a Wheel-Turning King and so forth without any defiled craving.
"Knowing skillful means" means knowing that all phenomena are ungraspable, which serves as the skillful means for becoming a Buddha.
Regarding "holy beings," this refers to the fact that the assemblies of all Buddhas are constantly present within birth.
It should be understood that these ten characteristics are present in every stage (*bhūmi*).
Having explained the ten characteristics of a bodhisattva’s entry into the stages, I shall next explain the characteristics of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) within the bodhisattva stages.
The verse says:
Having desire yet being free from the six obstacles, next possessing undisturbed wisdom,
neither drifting nor turning back, serving a spiritual friend and making offerings—
Dedicating [merit] leads to superior rebirth;
practicing virtue and engaging in play—such is the treasury of merit, the sixteenth mark of the Buddha’s son.
Commentary:
The various bodhisattvas attain the ten perfections within the stages, which possess sixteen characteristics.
What are these sixteen?
First, there is the presence of aspiration and delight, because they practice the various perfections.
Second is the absence of stinginess, because it is free from the hindrance to giving.
Third is the absence of contrariness, because it is free from the hindrance to ethical discipline.
Fourth is the absence of malice, because it is free from the hindrance to patience.
Fifth is indefatigability, because it removes obstacles to exertion.
Sixth is loving-kindness and compassion, because they remove obstacles to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Loving-kindness and compassion are able to bestow happiness and extract suffering; they are the antidotes to hatred and affliction, and they are attained through concentration.
Seventh is the absence of unwholesome wisdom (*dauṣprajña*), because it is free from the obstacles to wisdom.

There are three types of unwholesome wisdom: namely, conceptualization by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), conceptualization by recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), and conceptualization by manifestation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*); this [perfection] is able to sever them.
Eighth is undisturbed wisdom, because of being free from thoughts of other vehicles.
Ninth is not drifting, because one’s mind is not intoxicated by the superior pleasures of humans and devas.
Tenth is non-retrogression, because one’s mind does not regress due to the suffering of non-attainment or the suffering of difficult practices.
Eleventh is associating with spiritual friends, because one hears the Mahāyāna from virtuous mentors as shown by the Buddha.
Twelfth is making offerings, because one makes offerings to the Three Jewels.
Thirteenth is dedication, because of skillful means.

14. Superior Birth: This reveals the characteristic of the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), because one is free from the eight unfavorable conditions and never separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
15. Cultivation of Virtue: This reveals the characteristic of the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*), because one cultivates all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) without interruption.

The sixteenth is the mark of playful mastery of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), which reveals the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), because it signifies sporting in the merit of the great supernatural powers.
If a bodhisattva attains this mark, they become the foremost among all assemblies; these are called the sixteen marks of a son of the Buddha.
Having already explained the characteristics of the ten perfections within the Bodhisattva-bhūmi, the five virtues of each perfection shall now be explained.
The verse says:
At the time of ascending through each stage, Each perfection possesses five virtues.
"Two, two, and one— One should know that these pertain to both śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "at each stage of advancement, each perfection possesses five virtues," this means that when a bodhisattva cultivates each individual perfection within each respective bhūmi, every single perfection is endowed with five kinds of merit.
What are the five? First, the extinction of habitual tendencies; second, the attainment of tranquility; third, perfect luminosity; fourth, the arising of signs; and fifth, the extensive cause.
Regarding the extinction of habitual tendencies: it refers to the elimination, moment by moment, of the accumulation of habitual tendencies within the basis.
"Attaining serenity" means that by being free from various conceptual signs (*nimitta*), one attains the joy of the Dharma.
"Perfectly luminous" means that through the thorough knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākāra*), one does not engage in fragmented or partial understanding.
"The arising of signs" means that by entering the Great Ground (*mahābhūmi*), non-conceptual signs arise.

The "extensive cause" refers to fulfilling and purifying the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of wisdom for the sake of the *dharmakāya* of all aspects, thereby causing them to be gathered and increased.

Regarding the statement that "two, two, and one should be known as being associated with both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*," it should be understood here that the first two qualities belong to the category of *śamatha*, the next two qualities belong to the category of *vipaśyanā*, and the fifth quality belongs to both categories.
Having already explained the five merits for each of the perfections of the bodhisattva, I shall next explain the names of the ten bodhisattva stages.
The verse says:
Seeing the Truth and seeing the benefit of beings, In this stage, one attains Joyful Delight (pramuditā).
Transcending transgressions and transcending divergent thoughts—this is named the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (Vimalā).
Seeking the Dharma and maintaining the power of the Dharma, it produces illumination and is thus called the Ground of Radiance (Prabhākārī).
The fuel of the obstacles of affliction and the obstacles to knowledge—it can incinerate these, and is thus the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī).
There are two kinds of "hard to overcome": because it can overcome [the former], it is "Hard to Conquer.
Not dwelling in the contemplation of dual dharmas, it is constantly manifest, thus named "Manifest.
The mixed path is adjacent to the single path; because it travels far, it is named "Far-Going."
The perception of signs and the perception of signlessness, the moving and the immovable stage;
skillful in the power of the four analytical knowledges, he who speaks well is called "Good Wisdom.
The two gates pervade like clouds, raining down the Dharma—this is named the "Dharma Cloud."
The commentary states:

Regarding "seeing the truth and seeing the benefit of beings, one attains joy at this stage," it means that within the first bhūmi, the bodhisattva sees *tathatā* for the first time; that is, they see their own self-benefit. Having never seen it before, they now see it for the first time, and because they are close to *bodhi*.
Second is the vision of benefiting others, meaning the vision of altruism, because in each and every moment one is able to bring a hundred sentient beings to maturity.
Because these two visions give rise to supreme joy, it is called the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

Regarding the statement, "Emerging from transgressions and emerging from divergent thoughts is called the Stainless Ground (vimalā-bhūmi)": in the second ground, the bodhisattva emerges from two kinds of defilements—first, the defilement of violating the precepts, and second, the defilement of giving rise to thoughts associated with other vehicles (yāna).
Because it emerges from two defilements, it is called the Ground of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
As stated in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*:
"We should exert ourselves with diligence in order to attain and purify all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*)."

Regarding the statement that one is called "illuminated" because of seeking the Dharma, maintaining the power of the Dharma, and acting as an illumination: it means that within the third stage (*bhūmi*), the bodhisattva attains mastery over samādhi; thus, they are able to seek and maintain immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, and having attained the great illumination of the Dharma, they act as an illumination for others.
Because one is able to illuminate oneself and others through the Dharma, it is called the "Luminous Stage" (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).

Regarding the statement that "this 'Blazing Wisdom' (*arciṣmatī*) is that which can burn the fuel of the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations": in the fourth stage, the bodhisattva takes the wisdom of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) as the intrinsic nature of the flame, and takes the two obscurations—the afflictive and the cognitive—as the intrinsic nature of the fuel.
Because the bodhisattvas on this stage can give rise to the flames of wisdom to burn the fuel of the two obstacles, it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

Regarding "Difficult to Conquer" (*Sudurjayā*): because there are two kinds of things that can cause regression, it is difficult to conquer. For a bodhisattva on the fifth stage, there are two kinds of difficulties: first, the difficulty of laboring to transform sentient beings without the mind becoming weary; second, the difficulty of the mind not becoming weary when sentient beings do not follow one's transformation.
Because the bodhisattvas on this stage are able to overcome two difficulties and attain victory amidst those difficulties, it is named the "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā) stage.

Regarding the statement that they dwell in the constant manifestation of the contemplation of non-abiding in the two dharmas: by relying on the power of *prajñā* within the sixth stage, the bodhisattva is able to not abide in the two dharmas of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. This is called "manifest presence" (*abhimukhī*).
Because such insight (*vipaśyanā*) is constantly present before him, it is called the "Manifest" stage (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

Regarding the term "far-going" (*dūraṅgama*), it refers to one who has departed far from the mixed paths and is near the single path; thus, because the bodhisattva in the seventh stage is close to the path of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*), it is called "far-going."
Question:
Who is it that goes far away?
Answer:
Because the skillful means of effort reach their ultimate fulfillment here and one can travel far, it is called the Far-Going Ground (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).

Regarding "the ground unmoved by the movement of conceptualization of signs and conceptualization of signlessness": in the eighth stage, the Bodhisattva possesses both the conceptualization of signs and the conceptualization of signlessness accompanied by effort; since neither of these two conceptualizations can move them, and because they are free from such movement, it is called the Unmoving Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Regarding "the one who is skillful in speech through the power of the four analytical knowledges, well-renowned, and possessed of excellent wisdom": among the nine stages, the Bodhisattva’s four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are most preeminent. Within a single kṣaṇa, regarding all the various beings—humans and devas—within the three thousandfold world system, with their diverse species, diverse voices, diverse meanings, and diverse questions, a Bodhisattva of this stage can universally answer all these questions with a single voice and completely sever all doubts. Because he is thus said to be "skillful," it is named the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī*).

Regarding the phrase "the two gates are like clouds that rain down the Dharma everywhere, hence it is called the Cloud of Dharma": within the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva, by means of the gate of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the gate of mnemonic formulas (*dhāraṇī*), gathers all causes of the perfuming of what has been heard (*śruta-vāsanā*). These pervade the *ālaya-vijñāna* just as floating clouds pervade the empty sky. By means of this cloud of the perfuming of what has been heard, in every single moment, in every single mark (*lakṣaṇa*), in every single secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*), and in every single pore, they rain down immeasurable and boundless Dharma-rain, sufficing all sentient beings who are capable of being transformed.
Because it is able to rain down the Dharma like clouds and rain, it is called the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
Question:
Having explained the specific name, what is meant by "abiding" (*vihāra*)?
What is meant by "ground" (*bhūmi*)?
The verse says:
Because one gathers all roots of goodness and delights in dwelling [therein], it is called a "dwelling" (*vihāra*).
"Repeatedly counted as fearless, / They are further named after the stages (*bhūmi*).
The commentary explains:

"Because they are the joyful abodes for the accumulation of all roots of goodness, they are called 'abodes' (*vihāra*). This means that in order to accomplish various roots of goodness, Bodhisattvas joyfully abide in all stages at all times; therefore, the stages are designated as "abodes."
Regarding the fact that "fearlessness" (*abhaya*) is again designated by the name "ground" (*bhūmi*): *bhūmi* is composed of *bhu* and *mi*.
*Bhu* has the meaning of "repeatedly," and *mi* has the meaning of "actual number."
"Ya" (ye) signifies the meaning of fearlessness.
When Bodhisattvas desire to advance to higher stages, they repeatedly eliminate obstacles and repeatedly attain merits within each respective stage; this is called the meaning of "repeatedly."

The stages (bhūmi) take the number ten as their measure; within each individual stage, the bodhisattvas know the extent of the obstacles to be abandoned, know the extent of the qualities to be attained, and know that this is not in vain—this is called the meaning of "actual number."

The higher stages are places of fearlessness; because bodhisattvas fear the loss of the merits for the benefit of themselves and others within their own stage and thus strive to seek the higher stages, this is the meaning of fearlessness.
Because of these three meanings, it is called "ground" (*bhūmi*).
Having explained the names of the ten bodhisattva grounds, next the fourfold distinctions in the attainment of these grounds will be explained.
The verse says:
Through faith and through practice, Through realization and through attainment,
One should know that for all Bodhisattvas, There are four ways of attaining the stages (*bhūmi*).
Commentary:

There are four ways of attaining the stages (*bhūmi*): first, attainment through faith; second, attainment through practice; third, attainment through penetration; and fourth, attainment through fulfillment.
Regarding attainment through faith, it is because one attains the various stages by means of faith, as explained in the section on the Stage of Faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*).
Regarding "by practice," it is because one attains the various stages (*bhūmi*) through correct practice.
Bodhisattvas have ten types of correct practice regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma:

first, writing; second, making offerings; third, circulating; fourth, listening and receiving; fifth, reciting aloud; sixth, teaching others; seventh, practicing recitation; eighth, explaining; ninth, reflecting and discerning; tenth, cultivation.

These ten correct practices can generate an immeasurable mass of merit; because these practices lead to the attainment of the stages (*bhūmi*), they are called "attainment through practice" (*caryāpratilambha*).
As for "thorough penetration," it refers to penetrating the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); this stage extends up to the seventh ground and is thus termed "thorough penetration."
Regarding "attaining accomplishment," this refers to the attainment of accomplishment from the eighth stage up to the stage of Buddhahood.
Having already explained the four ways in which Bodhisattvas attain the stages, I shall now explain the distinctions among the four types of Bodhisattva practice.
The verse says:

The various perfections and factors of enlightenment, the supernormal powers and the means of integration—these serve both the Great and the Small Vehicles; they are entered together and accomplished together.

The commentary states: Generally speaking, all bodhisattva practices do not exceed four types: first, the practice of the perfections (pāramitā); second, the practice of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa); third, the practice of supernormal powers (abhijñā); and fourth, the practice of gathering sentient beings (saṃgraha).

The practice of the *pāramitās* is taught for the sake of sentient beings seeking the Mahāyāna; the practice of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) is taught for the sake of sentient beings seeking the Hīnayāna; the practice of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is taught to enable both types of sentient beings to enter the Buddha-dharma; and the practice of gathering sentient beings (*saṃgrahavastu*) is taught to bring both types of sentient beings to maturity in the Buddha-dharma.
The Chapter on Practice and Abiding is concluded.
Chapter Twenty-Four: Reverence for the Buddha. Commentary:
Having already explained the practice and abiding of bodhisattvas, the merit of paying homage to the Buddha will now be discussed.
The verse says:
To the one whose mind is both united with and detached from, Who never parts from the mind of benefiting others,
Who has compassion for all sentient beings— I prostrate to the Savior of the World.
The commentary states:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s immeasurable and supreme qualities.
"Harmonizing the mind" refers to the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), because it bestows happiness.
The mind of detachment is the mind of compassion, because it uproots suffering.
The non-detached mind is the mind of sympathetic joy, because it is constantly joyful.
The mind of benefit is the mind of equanimity, because it is free from defilement.
The verse says:
Liberated from all obscurations, Supreme over all worlds,
Pervading all places— I prostrate to the mind that is free from self.
The commentary states:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme merit in three respects.

"Liberation from all obstacles" manifests the excellence of liberation, because he has attained liberation from all afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and all cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
"Victorious over all worlds" manifests the excellence of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), because through mastery over the mind, one turns [the object] at will according to its focal point.
"Pervading all places" manifests the excellence of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), because wisdom pervades all objects.
By virtue of these three meanings, the mind attains liberation in three respects; therefore, it is called "liberation of the mind.
The verse says:
It can obstruct the arising of those afflictions, And it can also destroy those afflictions.
I pay homage with my head to the Compassionate One who purifies all defiled sentient beings.
Commentary:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme merit of being free from strife (*araṇa*).

Regarding "being able to prevent those afflictions from arising": although all sentient beings are prone to giving rise to afflictions, whatever actions the Tathāgata performs can cause them not to arise.
Furthermore, regarding "being able to destroy those afflictions": even if those afflictions have already arisen, the Tathāgata is also able to apply the skillful means of their antidotes.

If other persons possess the absence of contention (*araṇā*), they are only able to cause others not to give rise to afflictions by taking them as objects; however, they cannot cause those others to give rise to the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
The Tathāgata’s absence of contention is not like this: it not only causes others not to give rise [to afflictions], but can also cause them to give rise to the antidote; therefore, it is superior.

"I pay homage to the Compassionate One toward all defiled sentient beings" means that the Tathāgata’s *araṇā-samādhi* (the samādhi of non-contention) gives rise to universal compassion for all defiled sentient beings; therefore, he is called "the Compassionate One" with respect to them.
The verse says:
Effortless and unattached, Unimpeded and eternally tranquil,
Able to resolve all doubts— To you of supreme wisdom, I pay homage.
The commentary states:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme merit of the wisdom of his vows (*praṇidhijñāna*).
The Tathāgata’s wisdom of vows is superior by virtue of five factors:
First, effortless engagement; second, non-attachment to objects; third, unimpededness therein; fourth, perpetual tranquility; and fifth, the ability to resolve the doubts of the multitude.
By virtue of these five meanings, it is therefore superior.
As for the *praṇidhijñāna* (knowledge resulting from aspiration) of other persons: first, it is not effortless, because it arises through deliberate mental application (*manasikāra*);
second, it is not free from attachment, because it relies on the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Third, they are not unimpeded, because their knowledge is partial;
fourth, they are not eternally tranquil, because they do not abide in constant meditative concentration;
fifth, they do not resolve doubts, because they possess ignorance.
The verse says:
To the one who possesses unimpeded wisdom regarding the basis and that which is based upon it,
as well as regarding words and knowledge— the eloquent speaker, I pay homage.
The commentary states:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme, unimpeded qualities.
There are two aspects to what is taught:
First is the basis, namely the dharma;
second is that which depends upon it, namely the meaning.
There are two modes of exposition:
First is eloquence, second is skillful wisdom.
Regarding these—the speech and the instruments of speech—the Tathāgata’s wisdom is always unimpeded; therefore, he is supreme.
"Speech" here manifests his unimpeded activity.
Because it reveals the truth through skillful means, it is called "well-spoken.
The verse says:
It can cause one to depart and can cause one to hear; It knows practice and knows coming and going.
"I pay homage to the Teacher who causes them to attain liberation.
Commentary:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme merit of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The ability to go is the supernormal power of psychic travel (ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna), because one can proceed to various locations.
The ability to hear is the supernormal power of the divine ear (divya-śrotra), because one can hear various sounds.
"Knowing conduct" refers to the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*), for it is able to know the distinctions in the mental activities of others.

"Knowing whence they come" refers to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*), for it is able to know from what causes and conditions those people have come in their previous existences.

Knowing where [beings] go is the supernormal power of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādābhijñā*), because one knows that such-and-such a person has departed from this cause in the present life.
Causing them to attain deliverance is the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*), because one can teach the Dharma to them according to reality.
The verse says:
If sentient beings have a vision [of you], they know for certain that you are a Great Being (puruṣa).
Deeply conceiving pure faith, I pay homage to you with skillful means.
The commentary states:
This verse pays homage to the supreme merit of the Tathāgata’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

Should any sentient beings behold them, they immediately recognize the Tathāgata as a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) and give rise to the karma of pure faith toward the Tathāgata, by means of these marks and signs as a skillful expedient.
The verse says:
In grasping, relinquishing, abiding, and transformation, You have attained mastery through meditative concentration and wisdom;
To you, the World-Honored One, who possesses these four purities, I prostrate with my head.
The commentary states:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s pure and supreme qualities.
There are four kinds of purity:
First, purity of body; second, purity of object; third, purity of mind; fourth, purity of wisdom.
Regarding "taking, relinquishing, and abiding," this reveals the purity of body, because one attains mastery over taking, relinquishing, or abiding within the lifespan of one's own body.
"Transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) signifies the purity of the objective conditions, because one attains mastery over manifesting transformations and shifts among all objects.
"Concentration" (*samādhi*) signifies the purity of the mind, because one attains mastery over entering and emerging from all meditative absorptions.
"Wisdom" (jñāna) reveals the purity of wisdom, because it is able to know all objects without obstruction and attain mastery over them.
The verse says:
Skillful means and refuge, Purity and renunciation.
Having shattered the four deceptions therein, I prostrate to the Subduer of Māra.
Commentary:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme merit of power.
Māra destroys sentient beings by relying on four matters.
What are these four?
First, he relies on skillful means to deceive and delude sentient beings, saying that by indulging in the five sensory objects, one will be reborn in the good realms and not fall into the evil paths.
Second, they deceive sentient beings by relying on [false] refuge, claiming that Maheśvara and the like are the true objects of refuge while other places are not.
Third, they deceive sentient beings by relying on [false] purity, claiming that among the various meditative absorptions of the world, only these are pure while others are not.
The four reliances deceive sentient beings by claiming that the path and fruits of the Hīnayāna alone constitute liberation and that there is no Mahāyāna.
The Buddha, in order to destroy these four matters of Māra, revealed his own ten powers (*daśabala*).

First, by means of the power of knowledge regarding what is right and wrong (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), he destroys the first work of Māra: that one may attain birth in heaven through skillful means (*upāya*) and not through unskillful means.

Second, by means of the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (*karmasvakatā-jñānabala*), he destroys the second work of Māra: that one is born in heaven by virtue of one's own karma, and not by relying on the power of Īśvara or other such deities.

Third, one destroys the third matter of Māra through the power of knowledge regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because of possessing full knowledge of the meditative concentrations, liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*).

Fourth, one destroys the fourth matter of Māra through the latter seven powers of knowledge, because of causing those with inferior faculties and so forth to be separated [from lower states] and establishing those with superior faculties and so forth [in higher ones].
The verse says:
To the one who can explain wisdom and its abandonment, Detachment and its obstacles,
And who brings benefit to both self and others— I prostrate to you who crushes all that is false.
The commentary states:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme quality of fearlessness.
Regarding "the wise," this refers to the fearlessness of possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Regarding "abandonment," this refers to the fearlessness of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*).
Regarding "separation," this refers to the fearlessness of the path leading to the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanirodhagāminī-pratipad-vaiśāradya*).
Regarding "obstructions," this refers to the fearlessness concerning obstacles to the path (*antarāyikadharma-vaiśāradya*).

In this context, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) refer to the qualities of self-benefit, while "separation" (*viveka*) and "obstacles" (*āvaraṇa*) refer to the qualities of benefiting others.
If non-Buddhists were to raise the objection:

"The Gautama is not possessed of all-knowledge (*sarvajña*), he has not exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), the path he teaches cannot exhaust suffering, and the obstacles he describes cannot hinder the path."
The Tathāgata is able to subdue these four challenges; therefore, he is called "Fearless.
The verse says:
Even when subjected to the most severe punishments in the midst of the assembly, He has nothing to protect himself from.
I prostrate to the One who dwells correctly, free from the two defilements, and who gathers the assembly.
The commentary states:

"Because he inflicts the ultimate punishment upon the assembly while remaining personally without anything to protect"—this is a salutation to the Tathāgata’s supreme quality of non-protection (*arakṣa*). If he had anything to protect himself, he would be unable to pronounce the ultimate punishment within the assembly.

"Abiding correctly, free from the two defilements" refers to the preeminent merit of the Tathāgata’s foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). "Free from the two defilements" means being devoid of both joy and sorrow.
"Abiding correctly" means not forgetting mindfulness.
Because these two kinds of merit are superior, they are able to gather all followers; this is their activity.
The verse says:
In all places, whether walking or staying, there is nothing that is not [the domain of] omniscience.
I prostrate with my head to the Real Meaning who has severed all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Commentary:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme quality of having severed habitual tendencies.

In all places and at all times, whether walking, standing, or engaged in other activities, the Tathāgata’s every deportment is none other than that of omniscience, because he has completely eradicated all habitual tendencies of the afflictions.

If there were no Omniscient One, then even though afflictions might be exhausted, their habitual tendencies would not be; thus, while walking or staying, one might encounter a galloping chariot or a runaway horse and be harmed, because one’s deportment would lack the power of omniscience.
The Tathāgata does not possess such [faults], because he truly possesses omniscience.
The verse says:
In benefiting sentient beings, He acts according to the time without missing the proper moment.
His actions are always without error; I pay homage to him who is never forgetful.
Commentary:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme quality of being never forgetful.

The Tathāgata performs deeds that benefit sentient beings, always acting at the proper time and never missing the opportune moment; this is the activity of the non-forgetfulness dharma (*asammoṣadharmatā*).
Whatever the Tathāgata does is at all times true and not false; this is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the non-forgetfulness dharma.
The verse says:
Observing the realm of all sentient beings Six times throughout the day and night,
Because you are fully endowed with great compassion, I prostrate to you, O Benevolent One.
The commentary states:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme merit of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Because of his great compassion, the Tathāgata observes sentient beings during the six periods of day and night—seeing who is regressing and who is progressing—and causes those who have not yet produced roots of goodness to produce them, and those who have already produced roots of goodness to further increase them.

Although it is said to turn the wheel of Dharma six times a day, in reality, it turns the wheel of Dharma at all times and in every moment; because it is fully endowed with great compassion, this is the activity of great compassion.
To constantly give rise to the intention to benefit all sentient beings is the intrinsic nature of great compassion.
The verse says:
By way of conduct and by way of attainment, By way of wisdom and by way of activity—
To you who are supreme among all followers of the two vehicles, I pay homage with my head bowed.
The commentary states:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s uncommon and supreme qualities.
The Tathāgata possesses eighteen unshared dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*).

1. No failure in physical action; 2. No failure in verbal action; 3. No failure in mindfulness; 4. No divergent thoughts; 5. No unconcentrated mind; 6. No relinquishing without full awareness; 7. No decrease in desire for the Dharma; 8. No decrease in vigor; 9. No decrease in mindfulness; 10. No decrease in wisdom; 11. No decrease in liberation; 12. No decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation; 13. Wisdom that knows the past without attachment or obstruction; 14. Wisdom that knows the future without attachment or obstruction; 15. Wisdom that knows the present without attachment or obstruction; 16. Physical action follows the course of wisdom; 17. Verbal action follows the course of wisdom; 18. Mental action follows the course of wisdom.
In this context, by means of the practitioner, the six uncommon qualities of the first section are subsumed;
by means of attainment, the six uncommon qualities of the second section are subsumed;
and by means of wisdom, the three uncommon qualities of the third section are subsumed.
Regarding "by way of action," this subsumes the three unique qualities [of the Buddha] from the fourth section.
While all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are superior to all other sentient beings, the Tathāgata is superior even to them by virtue of these four unique qualities; therefore, he is called "supreme."
The verse says:
Because you have attained the Great Bodhi of the three bodies in all its aspects,
and because you can eliminate the doubts of sentient beings regarding all matters, I pay homage to you.
The commentary states:
This verse pays homage to the supreme merit of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Regarding the three bodies: first, the svabhāvakāya; second, the sambhogakāya; and third, the nirmāṇakāya. This explains the essential nature of the knowledge of all modes.
Question:
How is it that this wisdom knows all aspects regarding all objects?
Answer:
All sentient beings give rise to doubts in all circumstances; this wisdom can sever them—this is called the activity of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The verse says:
Unattached and faultless, Untainted and without cessation.
Unmoving and free from conceptual proliferation, I pay homage to the Pure One.
Commentary:
This verse pays homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme merit of perfected deliverance.
"Free from attachment" means being unstained by any material possessions.
"Free from transgression" means that one's physical and other actions are forever free from defilement.
"Free from impurity" means that the various sufferings of worldly dharmas do not turbidify the mind.
"Without cessation" means that because one has attained even a small measure [of realization], one does not abide therein.
"Without movement" means that the mind is constantly tranquil and not distracted.
"Without conceptual proliferation" means that all forms of discrimination regarding all phenomena do not arise.
The Tathāgata’s six perfections are called "pure" because they are fully endowed with the abandonment of the six obstacles.
The verse says:
Accomplishing the ultimate truth, Transcending all stages,
Having attained supreme honor among others, you liberate all sentient beings;
with inexhaustible and equal merits, you are fully endowed with them in the present.
The world sees you and the assembly sees you, yet neither humans nor devas can see [your ultimate nature].
The commentary states:
These two verses pay homage to the Tathāgata’s supreme merits regarding the marks of a Buddha.
Herein, the marks of a Buddha are briefly explained as being of six kinds:
First, the essence; second, the cause; third, the fruit; fourth, the activity; fifth, the association; sixth, the differentiation.
By means of these six aspects, one recognizes him as a Buddha; therefore, they are called the characteristics of a Buddha.
The "accomplishment of the ultimate truth" (paramārtha) is its essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), because it is accomplished through the most pure ultimate truth of suchness (*tathatā*).
The "departure from all stages" (*bhūmi*) is its causal characteristic, because it involves departing from all the bodhisattva stages.
"Attaining supreme honor among others" is the characteristic of the fruit, because one has attained the foremost position among all sentient beings.
"Liberating all sentient beings" is the characteristic of the activity, because one is able to cause all sentient beings to attain liberation.
The fact that inexhaustible and other such qualities are fully present in the present life constitutes the characteristic of correspondence (*saṃprayukta-lakṣaṇa*).
The fact that they are seen by the world, yet not seen by the multitudes of humans, devas, and others, constitutes the characteristic of distinction (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
"Seen by the world" means that all various worlds see it; this is the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).
"The assembly also sees it" means that the assembly of the Buddha’s great disciples also sees it; this is the saṃbhogakāya (enjoyment body).
"Unseen" means that it is never seen by anyone, including humans and devas; this is the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-nature body).
This constitutes the distinction between the three bodies (*trikāya*).
The Chapter on Reverencing the Buddha is hereby concluded.
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*, spoken at the time of ultimate purity, is hereby concluded.

In the thirteenth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*, the words and meanings remain; because the worldly ignorance and the turbidity of the seed-wisdom of Prajñā are great, the inferior mind gives rise to the dust of dharmas, thereby accomplishing the [defilement of the] Sūtra.
